In Kubernetes, this period may require at least 30 seconds for resource deletion and recreation. S3 clients typically include transparent retry mechanisms, such that they can resume operations during this period of time. Clients should experience minimal interruption, excluding scenarios which require taking the cluster entirely offline. Additional support For clusters that are significantly behind the latest stable release (6+ months), or for complex upgrade scenarios, consider using MinIO SUBNET for additional support and guidance during the upgrade procedure. If you encounter issues during the upgrade, see Troubleshooting upgrade issues.

title: Upgrade from open-source HyperVault on Kubernetes | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Upgrade from open-source HyperVault on Kubernetes

Use the steps in this document to upgrade a Helm-based cluster on Kubernetes using the HyperVault Community Operator and Object Store Tenants to HyperVault.

Upgrading from open-source HyperVault to HyperVault is permanent and cannot be reversed.

For airgapped environments or private registries, see the Airgapped environments procedure.

Prerequisites

Verify the following requirements have been met before doing the upgrade:

  1. Review the Before you begin section prior to starting the upgrade procedure.

  2. This procedure is tested against Operator and Tenant installations using the HyperVault Operator version 6.x.x or 7.x.x series. If you are using 5.x.x or earlier, reach out on SUBNET for further guidance or upgrade to one of the tested charts before upgrading.

  3. Upgrade requires that your Kubernetes user have at least cluster-admin permissions.

    HyperVault uses the ObjectStore resource where HyperVault uses Tenant.

    Note that the new CRD is only available after installing the HyperVault operator.

  4. Use helm version to verify that you are running a supported Helm version (v3.17 or later).

    If not, upgrade Helm to a supported version before completing the procedure.

Procedure

OpenShift users
OpenShift users should use oc instead of kubectl for all commands in this procedure. The commands are otherwise identical.

Install the HyperVault operator

Add the HyperVault Helm Repository to your local Helm configuration:

helm repo add hypervault https://helm.min.io

The repository contains the following charts for upgrade:

Chart Description
hypervault-operator Installs the HyperVault operator (replaces HyperVault Community operator).
hypervault-objectstore Installs HyperVault object storage (replaces HyperVault Tenant).
minkms-operator Installs the HyperVault Key Manager operator (optional, for encryption key management).
minkms Installs a Key Manager instance (optional).
directpv Installs DirectPV storage provisioner (optional, previously HyperVault Volume Manager).

The repository also includes older charts for legacy support. This table lists only the current charts.

Install the HyperVault operators

Refer to the operator values.yaml reference for a description of all possible options. You can run the following command to see the default values of the chart:

helm show values hypervault/hypervault-operator

If you are fine with the default settings, then continue to downloading the HyperVault license.

Do not copy the entire content and make changes. Create a new hypervault-operator-values.yaml file that only contains values different from the default.

Download the license

HyperVault needs a license to run. Download the license from SUBNET or request a free tier license from the HyperVault Pricing page.

Install the Helm chart

Install the HyperVault operator with your license. Replace LICENSE_HERE with your license value (beginning with eyJ...):

helm install --create-namespace --take-ownership -n hypervault hypervault \
     hypervault/hypervault-operator --set license="LICENSE_HERE"

If you created a customization file (hypervault-operator-values.yaml), add it to the command:

helm install --create-namespace --take-ownership -n hypervault hypervault \
     hypervault/hypervault-operator --set license="LICENSE_HERE" \
     -f hypervault-operator-values.yaml

The HyperVault operator automatically detects OpenShift environments in most cases. If automatic detection fails, you can force OpenShift mode using the global.forceOpenShift setting.

Install the operator (automatic detection):

helm install --create-namespace --take-ownership -n hypervault hypervault \
     hypervault/hypervault-operator --set license="LICENSE_HERE"

If you created a customization file (hypervault-operator-values.yaml), add it to the command:

helm install --create-namespace --take-ownership -n hypervault hypervault \
     hypervault/hypervault-operator --set license="LICENSE_HERE" \
     -f hypervault-operator-values.yaml

If automatic detection does not work, force OpenShift mode:

helm install --create-namespace --take-ownership -n hypervault hypervault \
     hypervault/hypervault-operator --set license="LICENSE_HERE" \
     --set global.forceOpenShift=true

OpenShift clusters with SELinux enabled may experience Pod startup failures when using large Persistent Volumes. For configuration guidance, see the SELinux configuration section in the OpenShift installation guide before proceeding with tenant upgrade.

The HyperVault operator installs to the hypervault namespace.

Validate installation

Check if all Pods in the hypervault namespace are running:

kubectl get all -n hypervault

The output should show running pods similar to the following:

NAME                                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f-hjbp5         1/1     Running   0          4m16s
pod/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85-kmwlv   1/1     Running   0          4m16s

NAME                            TYPE        CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)    AGE
service/object-store-operator   ClusterIP   10.43.210.230   <none>        4221/TCP   4m16s

NAME                                    READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
deployment.apps/adminjob-operator       1/1     1            1           4m16s
deployment.apps/object-store-operator   1/1     1            1           4m16s

NAME                                               DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
replicaset.apps/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f         1         1         1       4m16s
replicaset.apps/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85   1         1         1       4m16s

If you encounter PolicyBinding ownership errors during installation, upgrade your Helm version to 3.17 or later. If you cannot update Helm, see PolicyBinding ownership errors in the troubleshooting guide.

Upgrade HyperVault tenants to HyperVaults

The HyperVault Operator uses a Tenant resource to manage an object-store. HyperVault uses an ObjectStore resource that is compatible with but distinct from a Tenant. This procedure uses a HyperVault-provided upgrade tool to convert a Tenant to an object store.

Backup the Tenant resource

Run the following commands and save the output in a safe place:

kubectl get tenant -n $NAMESPACE $TENANT -o yaml > tenant-backup.yaml
kubectl get secrets -n $NAMESPACE -o yaml >> tenant-backup.yaml

Create hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

Creating the object store using the Helm chart requires a custom hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml. HyperVault provides an upgrade tool that helps create this file, based on your current tenant configuration. Run the following command to generate the objectstore-values.yaml:

docker run --pull=always --rm -v ~/.kube/config:/root/.kube/config  \
       quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator-migration:latest generate-helm \
           --namespace $NAMESPACE > hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

The upgrade tool needs to be able to connect to the Kubernetes cluster. Ensure the current Kubernetes context is set to the proper cluster.

Validate the generated hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml file

If you have access to SUBNET, create a ticket and upload both the tenant-backup.yaml and the hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml files. Experts at HyperVault can check if the generated file is correct and ready to proceed with the next step.

The upgrade tool attempts to perform checks on manually created resources (not managed by the HyperVault operator) and propose updates. For example, manually created services that may access HyperVault need to be updated. The upgrade tool creates TODO items in the generated values file.

All users should review the file to review and understand all the remarks in this file.

If you encounter issues running the upgrade tool, see Upgrade tool cannot connect to cluster in the troubleshooting guide.

Uninstall the old tenant

Delete the old Tenant resource using one of the methods below.

Deleting the Tenant disables the object store and introduces downtime. After deleting the Tenant resource, the StatefulSets, Services, and other resources will be deleted, but Persistent Volume Claims remain and will be used by the HyperVault.

The object store will not be available until it is recreated using the HyperVault ObjectStore resource. Always run this procedure on a staging environment to ensure you can detect and fix issues before deploying to production.

If the Tenant was installed using Helm, check the release name:

helm ls -n $NAMESPACE

Then uninstall the Helm release:

helm uninstall -n $NAMESPACE RELEASE_NAME

If the Tenant was not installed using Helm, manually delete it:

kubectl -n $NAMESPACE delete tenant $TENANT

Recreate the object-store

Use the following command to recreate the deleted tenant as a HyperVault:

helm install -n $NAMESPACE $TENANT hypervault/hypervault-objectstore -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml --take-ownership

Use --take-ownership to make sure it can recreate existing secrets.

Verify the new HyperVault is running

Check if the object store is up and running again.

kubectl -n $NAMESPACE get objectstore

The output should show Initialized.

Check that the object store is accessible, such as with mc admin info.

If the object store fails to reach Initialized status, see Object store fails to initialize after upgrade in the troubleshooting guide.

Uninstall HyperVault operator

After all object stores have been converted to use HyperVault operator, the old HyperVault operator can be removed.

The OSS HyperVault operator and HyperVault share the policybindings.sts.min.io CRD. When HyperVault is installed with --take-ownership, ownership annotations on the CRD are transferred to the HyperVault release, but the OSS operator’s stored Helm release still references the CRD. If the OSS operator is uninstalled with helm uninstall directly, Helm uses the stored manifest to delete the CRD, breaking HyperVault.

To prevent this, run the protect-crds command from the migration tool. It patches the OSS operator’s stored Helm release to add helm.sh/resource-policy: keep on the shared CRD:

docker run --pull=always --rm -v ~/.kube/config:/root/.kube/config \
       quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator-migration:latest protect-crds \
       --namespace $OSS_NAMESPACE --release $OSS_RELEASE

where $OSS_NAMESPACE and $OSS_RELEASE are the namespace and release name of the OSS Helm release (commonly hypervault and operator). The command is idempotent.

Once the stored manifest is patched, the OSS operator can be safely uninstalled:

helm uninstall -n $OSS_NAMESPACE $OSS_RELEASE

Helm will report that the shared CRD was kept, and HyperVault will continue to manage PolicyBinding resources.

Upgrading from OperatorHub to Helm (and vice-versa)

You can upgrade between OperatorHub and Helm installations using either a Helm-based approach or an OLM-based approach.

Helm-based upgrade

To upgrade using Helm, follow the standard upgrade procedure documented above on this page. This replaces the OperatorHub-managed operator with the Helm-managed HyperVault operator, then converts Tenants to ObjectStores.

OLM-based upgrade

If you prefer to continue using OperatorHub/OLM instead of Helm, follow these steps:

  1. Install the HyperVault Operator through OperatorHub (see installation documentation)

  2. Convert the Tenant resource to an ObjectStore resource using the upgrade tool

  3. Delete the existing Tenant resource (see Uninstall the old tenant section above)

  4. Deploy the new ObjectStore resource

  5. Verify installation (see Verify the new HyperVault is running section above)

  6. Uninstall the previous HyperVault operator through OperatorHub

Subpath considerations

Regardless of which upgrade approach you use, be aware that the default sub-path for Helm is set to data (pods mount /export0/data), while OperatorHub installations do not set this field (data is in /export0).

When upgrading from one system to another, the object-store may appear empty or IAM may seem to be reset. This is because it is fetching data from the incorrect directory.

Although root credentials will work, IAM will seem to be reset too. When upgrading from OperatorHub to Helm, you must explicitly set the subPath to ''.

For detailed guidance on this issue, see OperatorHub to Helm subpath issues in the troubleshooting guide.

If you encounter PolicyBinding ownership errors during installation, upgrade your Helm version to 3.17 or later. If you cannot update Helm, see PolicyBinding ownership errors in the troubleshooting guide.

Upgrade HyperVault tenants to HyperVaults

The HyperVault Operator uses a Tenant resource to manage an object-store. HyperVault uses an ObjectStore resource that is compatible with but distinct from a Tenant. This procedure uses a HyperVault-provided upgrade tool to convert a Tenant to an object store.

Backup the Tenant resource

Run the following commands and save the output in a safe place:

kubectl get tenant -n $NAMESPACE $TENANT -o yaml > tenant-backup.yaml
kubectl get secrets -n $NAMESPACE -o yaml >> tenant-backup.yaml

Create hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

Creating the object store using the Helm chart requires a custom hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml. HyperVault provides an upgrade tool that helps create this file, based on your current tenant configuration. Run the following command to generate the objectstore-values.yaml:

docker run --pull=always --rm -v ~/.kube/config:/root/.kube/config  \
       quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator-migration:latest generate-helm \
           --namespace $NAMESPACE > hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

The upgrade tool needs to be able to connect to the Kubernetes cluster. Ensure the current Kubernetes context is set to the proper cluster.

Validate the generated hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml file

If you have access to SUBNET, create a ticket and upload both the tenant-backup.yaml and the hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml files. Experts at HyperVault can check if the generated file is correct and ready to proceed with the next step.

The upgrade tool attempts to perform checks on manually created resources (not managed by the HyperVault operator) and propose updates. For example, manually created services that may access HyperVault need to be updated. The upgrade tool creates TODO items in the generated values file.

All users should review the file to review and understand all the remarks in this file.

If you encounter issues running the upgrade tool, see Upgrade tool cannot connect to cluster in the troubleshooting guide.

Uninstall the old tenant

Delete the old Tenant resource using one of the methods below.

Deleting the Tenant disables the object store and introduces downtime. After deleting the Tenant resource, the StatefulSets, Services, and other resources will be deleted, but Persistent Volume Claims remain and will be used by the HyperVault.

The object store will not be available until it is recreated using the HyperVault ObjectStore resource. Always run this procedure on a staging environment to ensure you can detect and fix issues before deploying to production.

If the Tenant was installed using Helm, check the release name:

helm ls -n $NAMESPACE

Then uninstall the Helm release:

helm uninstall -n $NAMESPACE RELEASE_NAME

If the Tenant was not installed using Helm, manually delete it:

kubectl -n $NAMESPACE delete tenant $TENANT

Recreate the object-store

Use the following command to recreate the deleted tenant as a HyperVault:

helm install -n $NAMESPACE $TENANT hypervault/hypervault-objectstore -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml --take-ownership

Use --take-ownership to make sure it can recreate existing secrets.

Verify the new HyperVault is running

Check if the object store is up and running again.

kubectl -n $NAMESPACE get objectstore

The output should show Initialized.

Check that the object store is accessible, such as with mc admin info.

If the object store fails to reach Initialized status, see Object store fails to initialize after upgrade in the troubleshooting guide.

Uninstall HyperVault operator

After all object stores have been converted to use HyperVault operator, the old HyperVault operator can be removed.

The OSS HyperVault operator and HyperVault share the policybindings.sts.min.io CRD. When HyperVault is installed with --take-ownership, ownership annotations on the CRD are transferred to the HyperVault release, but the OSS operator’s stored Helm release still references the CRD. If the OSS operator is uninstalled with helm uninstall directly, Helm uses the stored manifest to delete the CRD, breaking HyperVault.

To prevent this, run the protect-crds command from the migration tool. It patches the OSS operator’s stored Helm release to add helm.sh/resource-policy: keep on the shared CRD:

docker run --pull=always --rm -v ~/.kube/config:/root/.kube/config \
       quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator-migration:latest protect-crds \
       --namespace $OSS_NAMESPACE --release $OSS_RELEASE

where $OSS_NAMESPACE and $OSS_RELEASE are the namespace and release name of the OSS Helm release (commonly hypervault and operator). The command is idempotent.

Once the stored manifest is patched, the OSS operator can be safely uninstalled:

helm uninstall -n $OSS_NAMESPACE $OSS_RELEASE

Helm will report that the shared CRD was kept, and HyperVault will continue to manage PolicyBinding resources.

Upgrading from OperatorHub to Helm (and vice-versa)

You can upgrade between OperatorHub and Helm installations using either a Helm-based approach or an OLM-based approach.

Helm-based upgrade

To upgrade using Helm, follow the standard upgrade procedure documented above on this page. This replaces the OperatorHub-managed operator with the Helm-managed HyperVault operator, then converts Tenants to ObjectStores.

OLM-based upgrade

If you prefer to continue using OperatorHub/OLM instead of Helm, follow these steps:

  1. Install the HyperVault Operator through OperatorHub (see installation documentation)

  2. Convert the Tenant resource to an ObjectStore resource using the upgrade tool

  3. Delete the existing Tenant resource (see Uninstall the old tenant section above)

  4. Deploy the new ObjectStore resource

  5. Verify installation (see Verify the new HyperVault is running section above)

  6. Uninstall the previous HyperVault operator through OperatorHub

Subpath considerations

Regardless of which upgrade approach you use, be aware that the default sub-path for Helm is set to data (pods mount /export0/data), while OperatorHub installations do not set this field (data is in /export0).

When upgrading from one system to another, the object-store may appear empty or IAM may seem to be reset. This is because it is fetching data from the incorrect directory.

Although root credentials will work, IAM will seem to be reset too. When upgrading from OperatorHub to Helm, you must explicitly set the subPath to ''.

For detailed guidance on this issue, see OperatorHub to Helm subpath issues in the troubleshooting guide.

title: Upgrade from open-source HyperVault in Airgapped Environments | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Upgrade from open-source HyperVault in Airgapped Environments

Use the steps in this document to upgrade a Helm-based cluster on Kubernetes in an airgapped environment using the HyperVault Community Operator and Object Store Tenants to HyperVault.

Upgrading from open-source HyperVault to HyperVault is permanent and cannot be reversed.

When to use this procedure

This procedure is for environments where:

  • Kubernetes nodes do not have direct internet access
  • Container images must be mirrored to a private registry
  • Helm charts must be obtained through alternative means
  • Network restrictions prevent direct downloads from public repositories

Prerequisites

Verify the following requirements have been met before doing the upgrade:

  1. This procedure is tested against Operator and Tenant installations using the HyperVault Operator version 6.x.x or 7.x.x series. If you are using 5.x.x or earlier, reach out on SUBNET for further guidance or upgrade to one of the tested charts before upgrading.

  2. Upgrade requires that your Kubernetes user have at least cluster-admin permissions.

    HyperVault uses the ObjectStore resource where HyperVault uses Tenant.

    Note that this new CRD is only available AFTER installing the HyperVault operator.

  3. Use helm version to verify that you are running a supported Helm version (v3.17 or later).

    If not, upgrade Helm to a supported version before completing the procedure.

  4. You have access to both:

    • A system with internet access for downloading images and charts
    • Your private container registry for mirroring images

Phase 1: External preparation

Complete these steps on a system with internet access.

Download the Helm chart

Add the HyperVault Helm Repository and download the chart:

helm repo add hypervault https://helm.min.io
helm repo update
helm pull hypervault/hypervault-operator --version <VERSION>

Transfer the downloaded chart file to your airgapped environment.

Download container images

The HyperVault operator uses several container images that must be mirrored to your private registry.

  1. Identify required images:

    helm template hypervault/hypervault-operator | grep "image:" | sort -u

  2. Use skopeo to copy images to your private registry:

    skopeo copy docker://SOURCE_IMAGE docker://registry.example.local/TARGET_IMAGE

    Replace SOURCE_IMAGE with the original image reference and TARGET_IMAGE with your private registry path.

Download the upgrade tool

Copy the upgrade tool container to your private registry:

skopeo copy docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator-migration:latest \
            docker://registry.example.local/hypervault/operator-migration:latest

Phase 2: Airgapped upgrade

Complete these steps in your airgapped environment.

Configure service registries

HyperVault uses custom service registry configuration to simplify operations in airgapped environments. If you are using OpenShift, then you may also use the ImageDigestMirrorSet method. This document assumes the use of the HyperVault service registry method.

Create a repositories.yaml file to configure custom registries:

repositories:
  hypervault:
    hostname: registry.example.local
    pathPrefix: hypervault/
    # imagePullSecrets:
    # - name: hypervault-pull-secret-1
    # - name: hypervault-pull-secret-2

Replace registry.example.local with your private registry hostname and adjust the pathPrefix values to match your registry structure.

Create image pull secrets (if required)

If your private registry requires authentication, create image pull secrets:

kubectl create secret docker-registry hypervault-pull-secret-1 \
  --docker-server=registry.example.local \
  --docker-username=USERNAME \
  --docker-password=PASSWORD \
  --docker-email=EMAIL \
  -n hypervault

Uncomment and configure the imagePullSecrets section in repositories.yaml to reference these secrets.

Install the HyperVault operator

Refer to the operator values.yaml reference for a description of all possible options.

Create an hypervault-operator-values.yaml file with any custom values different from the default.

Download the license

HyperVault needs a license to run. Download the license from SUBNET or request a free tier license from the HyperVault Pricing page.

Install the Helm chart with custom registries

Install the HyperVault operator using the local chart and custom registry configuration. Replace LICENSE_HERE with your license value (beginning with eyJ...):

helm install --create-namespace --take-ownership -n hypervault hypervault \
     ./hypervault-operator-<VERSION>.tgz \
     -f repositories.yaml --set license="LICENSE_HERE"

If you created a customization file (hypervault-operator-values.yaml), add it to the command:

helm install --create-namespace --take-ownership -n hypervault hypervault \
     ./hypervault-operator-<VERSION>.tgz \
     -f repositories.yaml --set license="LICENSE_HERE" \
     -f hypervault-operator-values.yaml

The Helm chart uses the repositories.yaml values to update the HyperVault clusters. Because these clusters are static, if you need to redeploy with changed settings, use the following command:

helm upgrade -n hypervault hypervault ./hypervault-operator-<VERSION>.tgz \
             -f repositories.yaml --set license="LICENSE_HERE" \
             -f hypervault-operator-values.yaml

Check the output of the Helm command for the list of images to mirror.

If you encounter PolicyBinding ownership errors during installation, upgrade your Helm version to 3.17 or later. If you cannot update Helm, see PolicyBinding ownership errors in the troubleshooting guide.

Each operator uses a dedicated configuration map that holds the service configuration for each service. The Helm script installs these configuration maps. Use the following command to view them:

kubectl get configmap -n hypervault -o yaml
Do not change the values in the ConfigMap directly, as these will revert back to their original values when you run helm upgrade again later. Make all changes in the hypervault-operator-values.yaml file.

Validate installation

Check if all Pods in the hypervault namespace are running:

kubectl get pods -n hypervault

All pods should be in the running state after some initialization.

If you encounter issues running the upgrade tool, see Upgrade tool cannot connect to cluster in the troubleshooting guide.

Upgrade HyperVault tenants to HyperVaults

Follow the tenant upgrade procedure from the standard Kubernetes upgrade guide, with the following modifications for airgapped environments.

Generate upgrade values file

When running the upgrade tool, use your private registry:

docker run --pull=always --rm -v ~/.kube/config:/root/.kube/config \
       registry.example.local/hypervault/operator-migration:latest generate-helm \
             --namespace $NAMESPACE > hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

Replace registry.example.local with your private registry hostname.

Additional considerations

When creating your hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml file, ensure that:

  • All image references point to your private registry.
  • Image pull secrets are configured if required.
  • The repository configuration matches your repositories.yaml settings.
  • Use the downloaded charts instead of the HyperVault Helm repository.

All other upgrade steps remain the same as the standard Kubernetes procedure.

If the object store fails to reach Initialized status, see Object store fails to initialize after upgrade in the troubleshooting guide. In airgapped environments, this is often caused by image pull errors due to missing or incorrectly configured private registry references.

title: Upgrade from open-source HyperVault in Airgapped Environments | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Upgrade from open-source HyperVault in Airgapped Environments

Use the steps in this document to upgrade a Helm-based cluster on Kubernetes in an airgapped environment using the HyperVault Community Operator and Object Store Tenants to HyperVault.

Upgrading from open-source HyperVault to HyperVault is permanent and cannot be reversed.

When to use this procedure

This procedure is for environments where:

  • Kubernetes nodes do not have direct internet access
  • Container images must be mirrored to a private registry
  • Helm charts must be obtained through alternative means
  • Network restrictions prevent direct downloads from public repositories

Prerequisites

Verify the following requirements have been met before doing the upgrade:

  1. This procedure is tested against Operator and Tenant installations using the HyperVault Operator version 6.x.x or 7.x.x series. If you are using 5.x.x or earlier, reach out on SUBNET for further guidance or upgrade to one of the tested charts before upgrading.

  2. Upgrade requires that your Kubernetes user have at least cluster-admin permissions.

    HyperVault uses the ObjectStore resource where HyperVault uses Tenant.

    Note that this new CRD is only available AFTER installing the HyperVault operator.

  3. Use helm version to verify that you are running a supported Helm version (v3.17 or later).

    If not, upgrade Helm to a supported version before completing the procedure.

  4. You have access to both:

    • A system with internet access for downloading images and charts
    • Your private container registry for mirroring images

Phase 1: External preparation

Complete these steps on a system with internet access.

Download the Helm chart

Add the HyperVault Helm Repository and download the chart:

helm repo add hypervault https://helm.min.io
helm repo update
helm pull hypervault/hypervault-operator --version <VERSION>

Transfer the downloaded chart file to your airgapped environment.

Download container images

The HyperVault operator uses several container images that must be mirrored to your private registry.

  1. Identify required images:

    helm template hypervault/hypervault-operator | grep "image:" | sort -u

  2. Use skopeo to copy images to your private registry:

    skopeo copy docker://SOURCE_IMAGE docker://registry.example.local/TARGET_IMAGE

    Replace SOURCE_IMAGE with the original image reference and TARGET_IMAGE with your private registry path.

Download the upgrade tool

Copy the upgrade tool container to your private registry:

skopeo copy docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator-migration:latest \
            docker://registry.example.local/hypervault/operator-migration:latest

Phase 2: Airgapped upgrade

Complete these steps in your airgapped environment.

Configure service registries

HyperVault uses custom service registry configuration to simplify operations in airgapped environments. If you are using OpenShift, then you may also use the ImageDigestMirrorSet method. This document assumes the use of the HyperVault service registry method.

Create a repositories.yaml file to configure custom registries:

repositories:
  hypervault:
    hostname: registry.example.local
    pathPrefix: hypervault/
    # imagePullSecrets:
    # - name: hypervault-pull-secret-1
    # - name: hypervault-pull-secret-2

Replace registry.example.local with your private registry hostname and adjust the pathPrefix values to match your registry structure.

Create image pull secrets (if required)

If your private registry requires authentication, create image pull secrets:

kubectl create secret docker-registry hypervault-pull-secret-1 \
  --docker-server=registry.example.local \
  --docker-username=USERNAME \
  --docker-password=PASSWORD \
  --docker-email=EMAIL \
  -n hypervault

Uncomment and configure the imagePullSecrets section in repositories.yaml to reference these secrets.

Install the HyperVault operator

Refer to the operator values.yaml reference for a description of all possible options.

Create an hypervault-operator-values.yaml file with any custom values different from the default.

Download the license

HyperVault needs a license to run. Download the license from SUBNET or request a free tier license from the HyperVault Pricing page.

Install the Helm chart with custom registries

Install the HyperVault operator using the local chart and custom registry configuration. Replace LICENSE_HERE with your license value (beginning with eyJ...):

helm install --create-namespace --take-ownership -n hypervault hypervault \
     ./hypervault-operator-<VERSION>.tgz \
     -f repositories.yaml --set license="LICENSE_HERE"

If you created a customization file (hypervault-operator-values.yaml), add it to the command:

helm install --create-namespace --take-ownership -n hypervault hypervault \
     ./hypervault-operator-<VERSION>.tgz \
     -f repositories.yaml --set license="LICENSE_HERE" \
     -f hypervault-operator-values.yaml

The Helm chart uses the repositories.yaml values to update the HyperVault clusters. Because these clusters are static, if you need to redeploy with changed settings, use the following command:

helm upgrade -n hypervault hypervault ./hypervault-operator-<VERSION>.tgz \
             -f repositories.yaml --set license="LICENSE_HERE" \
             -f hypervault-operator-values.yaml

Check the output of the Helm command for the list of images to mirror.

If you encounter PolicyBinding ownership errors during installation, upgrade your Helm version to 3.17 or later. If you cannot update Helm, see PolicyBinding ownership errors in the troubleshooting guide.

Each operator uses a dedicated configuration map that holds the service configuration for each service. The Helm script installs these configuration maps. Use the following command to view them:

kubectl get configmap -n hypervault -o yaml
Do not change the values in the ConfigMap directly, as these will revert back to their original values when you run helm upgrade again later. Make all changes in the hypervault-operator-values.yaml file.

Validate installation

Check if all Pods in the hypervault namespace are running:

kubectl get pods -n hypervault

All pods should be in the running state after some initialization.

If you encounter issues running the upgrade tool, see Upgrade tool cannot connect to cluster in the troubleshooting guide.

Upgrade HyperVault tenants to HyperVaults

Follow the tenant upgrade procedure from the standard Kubernetes upgrade guide, with the following modifications for airgapped environments.

Generate upgrade values file

When running the upgrade tool, use your private registry:

docker run --pull=always --rm -v ~/.kube/config:/root/.kube/config \
       registry.example.local/hypervault/operator-migration:latest generate-helm \
             --namespace $NAMESPACE > hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

Replace registry.example.local with your private registry hostname.

Additional considerations

When creating your hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml file, ensure that:

  • All image references point to your private registry.
  • Image pull secrets are configured if required.
  • The repository configuration matches your repositories.yaml settings.
  • Use the downloaded charts instead of the HyperVault Helm repository.

All other upgrade steps remain the same as the standard Kubernetes procedure.

If the object store fails to reach Initialized status, see Object store fails to initialize after upgrade in the troubleshooting guide. In airgapped environments, this is often caused by image pull errors due to missing or incorrectly configured private registry references.

title: Upgrade from open-source HyperVault on Linux | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Upgrade from open-source HyperVault on Linux

Use the steps in this document to upgrade a cluster on Linux from open-source HyperVault clusters (AGPL3.0) to HyperVault.

Considerations

Upgrading from open-source HyperVault to HyperVault is permanent and cannot be reversed. Once upgraded, the cluster cannot be reverted to open-source HyperVault.

Upgrading to HyperVault on Linux requires minimal downtime for binary replacement and restart. Recent versions of HyperVault support storing the license directly in the object store, eliminating the need to configure license files on each host.

Upgrade Procedure

Review the Before you begin section prior to starting the upgrade procedure.

  1. Back up cluster metadata

    Use the mc admin config export, mc admin cluster bucket export, and mc admin cluster iam export commands to take a snapshot of the cluster configurations:

    mc admin config export ALIAS_NAME > hypervault-prod-config.txt
mc admin cluster bucket export ALIAS_NAME
mc admin cluster iam export ALIAS_NAME

    The commands create the following files in the current folder:

    File name Contents
    hypervault-prod-config.txt Cluster configuration
    ALIAS_NAME-bucket-metadata.zip Bucket metadata
    ALIAS_NAME-iam-info.zip IAM metadata

    Save all files to a secure location.

  2. Download the HyperVault binary

    Download the latest stable HyperVault binary for Linux. The command overwrites the existing hypervault binary at that path. Use the command appropriate for your host system CPU architecture.

    Use the following commands to download the binary for AMD64 architectures and mark the binary as executable.

    curl --retry 10 --progress-bar -L https://dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/linux-amd64/hypervault -o hypervault
chmod +x ./hypervault

    Use the following commands to download the binary for ARM64 architectures and mark the binary as executable.

    curl --retry 10 --progress-bar -L https://dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/linux-arm64/hypervault -o hypervault
chmod +x ./hypervault

  3. Replace the older binary on each node

    Overwrite the existing binary in /usr/local/bin with the downloaded HyperVault binary, using root permissions if necessary.

    sudo mv -f ./hypervault /usr/local/bin/hypervault

    Repeat for all nodes in the cluster.

  4. Restart the cluster

    Use mc admin service restart to restart all nodes in the cluster simultaneously. Rolling or one-at-a-time restarts may produce undesired behavior as nodes start up with incompatible binaries.

    mc admin service restart ALIAS_NAME

    Monitor the status of the cluster using journalctl -uf hypervault. Once all nodes reach healthy status, validate the upgrade version using mc admin info.

  5. Register the license

    Download your license from SUBNET or request a free tier license from the HyperVault Pricing Page.

    Choose one of the following methods to register your license:

    Register the license with the cluster using the mc license register command:

    mc license register ALIAS_NAME --license LICENSE_FILE

    Replace LICENSE_FILE with the path to your downloaded license file.

    The license is stored in the object store and automatically replicated across all nodes.

    Configure the license with the HYPERVAULT_LICENSE environment variable:

    1. Copy your license file to /opt/hypervault/hypervault.license on each host machine
    2. Ensure the hypervault-user user and group have read access to the file and path
    3. Add HYPERVAULT_LICENSE=/opt/hypervault/hypervault.license to /etc/default/hypervault on all hosts
    4. Restart the cluster with mc admin service restart ALIAS_NAME

    This method requires managing the license file on each host. The file must be identical across all nodes.

    If HyperVault fails to start due to configuration issues, see HyperVault fails to start after Linux upgrade for instructions on importing your backup configurations.

title: Troubleshooting Upgrade Issues | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Troubleshooting Upgrade Issues

This page documents common issues encountered when upgrading from open-source HyperVault to HyperVault and their solutions.

KES root CA certificate changes

The ObjectStore CRD has subtle changes in dealing with CA certificates for KES compared to the HyperVault Community Operator.

Problem

The HyperVault Community Operator does not support adding CA certificates to the KES container. This often resulted in adding a client certificate that was used as a CA certificate.

Old configuration (open-source HyperVault)

The following KES configuration illustrates the previous approach:

kes:
  replicas: 2
  configuration:
    address: :7373
    admin:
      identity: ${HYPERVAULT_KES_IDENTITY}
    tls:
      key: /tmp/kes/server.key    # Path to the TLS private key
      cert: /tmp/kes/server.crt   # Path to the TLS certificate
    keystore:
      vault:
        endpoint: "https://vault.example.com"
        engine: "kv"
        version: "v2"
        approle:
          engine: ""
          id: "app-role-id"
          secret: "app-role-secret"
          retry: 15s
        tls:        # The Vault client TLS configuration for mTLS authentication and certificate verification
          key: ""     # Path to the TLS client private key for mTLS authentication to Vault
          cert: ""    # Path to the TLS client certificate for mTLS authentication to Vault
          ca: "/tmp/kes/vaultroot-ca.crt"      # Path to one or multiple PEM root CA certificates
        status:     # Vault status configuration. The server will periodically reach out to Vault to check its status.
          ping: 10800s   # Duration until the server checks Vault's status again.
  clientCertSecret:
    name: vaultroot-ca
    type: opaque

Solution

HyperVault does not allow this method. You must add any CA certificate using the trustedCAs field. This mounts the CA certificate in the Pod as a system root CA, so KES trusts certificates signed using that CA.

New configuration (HyperVault)

In HyperVault this configuration should look like this:

kes:
  replicas: 2
  configuration:
    address: :7373
    admin:
      identity: ${HYPERVAULT_KES_IDENTITY}
    tls:
      key: /tmp/kes/server.key    # Path to the TLS private key
      cert: /tmp/kes/server.crt   # Path to the TLS certificate
    keystore:
      vault:
        endpoint: "https://vault.example.com"
        engine: "kv"
        version: "v2"
        approle:
          engine: ""
          id: "app-role-id"
          secret: "app-role-secret"
          retry: 15s
        # The entire TLS section can be removed, because CA certificate is trusted as a system root CA
  trustedCAs:
    name: vaultroot-ca
    type: opaque

HyperVault requires certificates to be named public.crt (for type opaque). Client certificates often used arbitrary names (the example used vaultroot-ca.crt).

To resolve this, edit the secret to rename the certificate field to public.crt:

In the editor that opens, locate the data: section and rename the certificate field from its current name (for example, vaultroot-ca.crt) to public.crt. Save and exit the editor to apply the changes.

OperatorHub to Helm subpath issues

Problem

When upgrading from OperatorHub to Helm (or vice-versa), the object store appears empty or IAM seems to be reset.

Cause

The default sub-path for Helm is set to data, so all pods mount /export0/data. The OperatorHub installation does not set this field, so all data is in /export0.

When upgrading from one system to another, the object store fetches data from the incorrect directory. Although root credentials will work, IAM will seem to be reset.

Solution

When upgrading from OperatorHub to Helm, you must explicitly set the subPath to an empty string in your hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml:

pools:

Problem

Cause

Solution

If using Helm 3.17 or later, use the --take-ownership flag:

helm install --take-ownership -n hypervault hypervault hypervault/hypervault-operator ...

If using an older version of Helm that does not support --take-ownership, manually patch the CRD:

kubectl patch crd policybindings.sts.min.io --type='merge' \
     -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"meta.helm.sh/release-name":"hypervault","meta.helm.sh/release-namespace":"hypervault"}}}'

Make sure the release name and namespace match your helm install command.

Problem

HyperVault operator cannot connect to or manage the object stores anymore after uninstalling the HyperVault operator.

Cause

If the policybindings.sts.min.io CRD is not protected before you uninstall the HyperVault operator with Helm, the uninstall may remove the CRD. The HyperVault operator uses policy bindings to connect to the object-store, so it cannot work without this CRD.

Solution

Problem

The upgrade tool fails with connection errors when trying to generate the hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml file.

Cause

The upgrade tool needs access to your Kubernetes cluster to read the current Tenant configuration. The current Kubernetes context may not be set correctly, or the kubeconfig may not be accessible.

Solution

  1. Verify your current Kubernetes context:

    kubectl config current-context

  2. Switch to the correct context if needed:

    kubectl config use-context CONTEXT_NAME

  3. Ensure the upgrade tool can access your kubeconfig:

    docker run --pull=always --rm -v ~/.kube/config:/root/.kube/config \
       quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator-migration:latest generate-helm \
                                              --namespace $NAMESPACE

  4. For airgapped environments, ensure you are using the correct registry path:

    docker run --pull=always --rm -v ~/.kube/config:/root/.kube/config \
       registry.example.local/hypervault/operator-migration:latest generate-helm \
                                              --namespace $NAMESPACE

Object store fails to initialize after upgrade

Problem

After upgrading and recreating the object store, the ObjectStore resource does not reach Initialized status.

Cause

This can occur for several reasons:

  • Persistent Volume Claims were not preserved correctly
  • Configuration secrets are missing or incorrect
  • License is invalid or not properly configured
  • Resource constraints prevent pods from starting

Solution

  1. Check the ObjectStore status:

    kubectl -n $NAMESPACE get objectstore
kubectl -n $NAMESPACE describe objectstore $OBJECTSTORE_NAME

  2. Check pod status and logs:

    kubectl -n $NAMESPACE get pods
kubectl -n $NAMESPACE logs POD_NAME

  3. Verify Persistent Volume Claims exist:

    kubectl -n $NAMESPACE get pvc

  4. Verify the configuration secret exists and is correct:

    kubectl -n $NAMESPACE get secret storage-configuration -o yaml

  5. Check the license is properly configured in the operator:

    kubectl -n hypervault get secret hypervault-license -o yaml

HyperVault fails to start after Linux upgrade

Problem

After upgrading from open-source HyperVault to HyperVault on Linux, the HyperVault server fails to start or shows errors related to configuration or metadata.

Cause

HyperVault may fail to automatically upgrade configurations from very old HyperVault versions. The server may be unable to read or parse older configuration formats, bucket metadata, or IAM settings.

Solution

Use the backup files created at the beginning of the upgrade procedure to manually import the configurations:

  1. Import the cluster configuration:

    mc admin config import ALIAS_NAME < hypervault-prod-config.txt

  2. Import bucket metadata:

    mc admin cluster bucket import ALIAS_NAME ALIAS_NAME-bucket-metadata.zip

  3. Import IAM metadata:

    mc admin cluster iam import ALIAS_NAME ALIAS_NAME-iam-info.zip

Replace ALIAS_NAME with your cluster’s alias and ensure the filenames match those created during the backup step.

After importing, restart the HyperVault service and verify it starts successfully:

mc admin service restart ALIAS_NAME
mc admin info ALIAS_NAME

Additional resources

If you encounter issues not covered here or need additional assistance:

  1. Review the generated hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml for TODO items that need attention.
  2. Check the Release Notes for known issues.
  3. Contact HyperVault SUBNET for expert support.
  4. Create a ticket and upload both tenant-backup.yaml and hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml for review.

  replicas: 2
  configuration:
    address: :7373
    admin:
      identity: ${HYPERVAULT_KES_IDENTITY}
    tls:
      key: /tmp/kes/server.key    # Path to the TLS private key
      cert: /tmp/kes/server.crt   # Path to the TLS certificate
    keystore:
      vault:
        endpoint: "https://vault.example.com"
        engine: "kv"
        version: "v2"
        approle:
          engine: ""
          id: "app-role-id"
          secret: "app-role-secret"
          retry: 15s
        tls:        # The Vault client TLS configuration for mTLS authentication and certificate verification
          key: ""     # Path to the TLS client private key for mTLS authentication to Vault
          cert: ""    # Path to the TLS client certificate for mTLS authentication to Vault
          ca: "/tmp/kes/vaultroot-ca.crt"      # Path to one or multiple PEM root CA certificates
        status:     # Vault status configuration. The server will periodically reach out to Vault to check its status.
          ping: 10800s   # Duration until the server checks Vault's status again.
  clientCertSecret:
    name: vaultroot-ca
    type: opaque

HyperVault does not allow this method. You must add any CA certificate using the trustedCAs field. This mounts the CA certificate in the Pod as a system root CA, so KES trusts certificates signed using that CA.

      key: /tmp/kes/server.key    # Path to the TLS private key
      cert: /tmp/kes/server.crt   # Path to the TLS certificate

      vault:
        endpoint: "https://vault.example.com"
        engine: "kv"
        version: "v2"

          engine: ""
          id: "app-role-id"
          secret: "app-role-secret"

    name: vaultroot-ca
    type: opaque

title: Upgrade HyperVault on Kubernetes (Helm) | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Upgrade HyperVault on Kubernetes (Helm)

Upgrade HyperVault Helm clusters on Kubernetes infrastructure.

Overview

HyperVault Helm installations consist of two primary components:

  1. Operator Chart - Controls resources like CustomResourceDefinitions and core operator functionality
  2. Object Store Chart - Deploys and manages HyperVault instances

Upgrades involve updating these charts and deploying new container images. The exact procedure depends on your cluster environment’s network configuration and registry access.

The HyperVault Operator upgrades an object store one pod at a time, so the cluster keeps serving requests for the whole upgrade. Each pod finishes the requests it is already handling before it stops, up to the number of seconds set in rollingTimeoutSeconds, which defaults to 600. A request still running when that period expires is cut off, so raise the value if your workload has requests longer than ten minutes.

Clients connected to a pod that restarts do reconnect, and a load balancer sends them to a pod that is still running. Most S3 SDKs retry failed operations, so applications generally do not surface an error.

Upgrading to or from a release earlier than RELEASE.2025-12-20T04-58-37Z replaces every pod at once instead, which stops the cluster until the pods come back.

For how this compares with restarting every node at once, and how to choose between them on Linux, see Choose a restart mode.

Prerequisites

Before upgrading in any environment:

  • Review the upgrade prerequisites
  • Back up your existing Helm configurations
  • Ensure you have a valid, current HyperVault license
  • Verify the health of your current cluster
  • Review release notes for breaking changes

See the scenario-specific guides above for detailed prerequisites and step-by-step instructions.

Choose your cluster scenario

Select the upgrade guide that matches your environment:

Your cluster has direct internet access to helm.min.io and quay.io and uses the public Helm repository and container registries.

See the Upgrade with Public Registries procedure for detailed steps.

This is the simplest upgrade path with the fewest steps.

Your cluster uses a private container registry but has internet access to helm.min.io for downloading Helm charts.

See the Upgrade with Private Registry procedure for detailed steps.

This scenario requires copying container images to your private registry before deploying chart updates.

Your cluster has no direct internet access. You must prepare all artifacts (container images and Helm charts) on an external system before transferring them to your environment.

See the Upgrade in Airgapped Environment procedure for detailed steps.

This scenario requires the most preparation, with steps split between an internet-connected system and your airgapped environment.

Common upgrade concepts

Regardless of your cluster scenario, HyperVault upgrades follow this general workflow:

  1. Update Operator Chart - Upgrade the operator chart and deploy the new operator image
  2. Update Object Store Chart - Upgrade the object store chart and deploy new object store images
  3. Bump the API version - Synchronize the API version across all nodes after the upgrade

You can also upgrade only the HyperVault Object Store image version without updating the chart itself if you only need to update the running software version.

Do not upgrade the operator by image alone

The image-only shortcut above applies to the HyperVault Object Store image, not to the operator.

Always upgrade the operator through its Helm chart. That chart owns the operator’s RBAC (its ClusterRole and bindings) and the CustomResourceDefinitions, and keeps them in sync with the operator version. If you replace only the operator image and leave the chart in place, those resources stay at the previous version.

When a newer operator needs permissions or CRD fields that the older chart never created, the operator cannot finish syncing its informer caches. Its reconcile workers never start, and object store rollouts stall until you upgrade to the matching operator chart.

title: Upgrade HyperVault on Linux | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Upgrade HyperVault on Linux

This page documents upgrade procedures for HyperVault Server clusters on bare-metal Linux infrastructure.

Each procedure below replaces the binary on every node and then restarts the cluster. Decide how you want the cluster to restart before you start. By default all nodes restart at the same time, which typically finishes in under 3 seconds and is the mode HyperVault recommends. A rolling restart keeps the cluster serving throughout but takes longer, requires a load balancer, and still reconnects the clients attached to each restarting server. See Choose a restart mode.

In site-replicated deployments, Security Token Service (STS) tokens are signed with the site replicator service account credentials rather than the root credentials.

Any STS tokens previously signed by root credentials are no longer valid after upgrading to a version that includes this change. After the upgrade, clients must regenerate their STS tokens as usual.

Upgrade HyperVault using DEB or RPM

Use these steps to upgrade a HyperVault cluster where the server process is managed by systemctl, such as those created using the HyperVault DEB/RPM packages.

This procedure assumes you have the HYPERVAULT_CONFIG_ENV_FILE variable set on all HyperVault nodes.

  1. Update the HyperVault binary on each node

    Use the following commands to download the latest stable HyperVault RPM and update the existing installation. Use the command appropriate for your host system CPU architecture.

    The package is now named hypervault rather than hypervault, and it obsoletes and replaces the older hypervault package. Use dnf install rather than dnf update, which matches on the installed package name and does not process the rename. The download URL is unchanged.

    AMD64

    curl --retry 10 --progress-bar -L  "https://dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/linux-amd64/hypervault.rpm" -o hypervault.rpm
sudo dnf install hypervault.rpm

    ARM64

    curl --retry 10 --progress-bar -L  "https://dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/linux-arm64/hypervault.rpm" -o hypervault.rpm
sudo dnf install hypervault.rpm

    Use the following commands to download the latest stable HyperVault DEB and upgrade the existing installation. Use the command appropriate for your host system CPU architecture.

    AMD64

    curl --retry 10 --progress-bar -L  "https://dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/linux-amd64/hypervault.deb" -o hypervault.deb
sudo dpkg -i hypervault.deb

    ARM64

    curl --retry 10 --progress-bar -L  "https://dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/linux-arm64/hypervault.deb" -o hypervault.deb
sudo dpkg -i hypervault.deb

    Run hypervault --version on each node to validate that you successfully upgraded all binaries to the same version. Do not proceed unless all nodes use the same HyperVault binary version.

  2. Restart the cluster

    Run the mc admin service restart command to restart the server processes in the cluster.

    To restart every server at the same time, run:

    mc admin service restart ALIAS

    To keep the cluster serving requests throughout, add --rolling with a graceful wait period:

    mc admin service restart ALIAS --rolling 2m

    Replace ALIAS with the alias of the HyperVault cluster to restart.

    Without --rolling, every server restarts at the same time. The restart typically completes in under 3 seconds, and S3 clients reconnect on their own, so applications generally do not notice it.

    With --rolling, the servers restart in sequence and the cluster keeps serving throughout, provided a load balancer routes new requests away from each server while it restarts. Clients already connected to a restarting server still reconnect, because a load balancer cannot move an established connection. See Choose a restart mode.

  3. Validate the upgrade

    Use the mc admin info command to check that all HyperVault servers are online, operational, and reflect the installed HyperVault version.

  4. Upgrade HyperVault Client

    Upgrade your mc binary to match or closely follow the server release. You can use the mc update command to update the binary to the latest stable release:

    mc update

  5. Bump the API version

    Starting with RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, the cluster leader automatically advances the cluster to the latest API version after a rolling upgrade that changes the API version. By default, the bump happens immediately once all nodes are online and support the latest version. If some nodes are temporarily absent, the cluster tolerates their absence for up to one hour before committing the bump.

    Automatic bumping is enabled by default. To disable it and manage the API version manually, set HYPERVAULT_API_AUTO_BUMP=off on all nodes before upgrading.

    Starting with RELEASE.2026-07-24T16-43-31Z, you can delay the bump instead of disabling it. Set HYPERVAULT_API_BUMP_BAKE_TIME on all nodes to a duration, for example 1h, to configure a bake time. The cluster then holds the previous API version for that long after it is fully upgraded. The bump commits once all nodes have stayed online on the newer release for that duration. The bake time applies only while every node is online. If a node drops out, the cluster commits the bump once the remaining quorum has held the newer release for one hour, however long a bake time you configured, so a longer rollback window depends on keeping every node online for it. During the bake time, the cluster keeps writing data in the previous version’s format, so downgrading the server binary remains safe. The default is 0, which commits the bump immediately. A bake time applies only while automatic bumping is enabled. Features that require the new API version stay inactive until the bump commits, so a longer bake time also delays their availability.

    When automatic bumping is disabled, or when upgrading to a release earlier than RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, run the following command once all nodes are running the new version:

    mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api

    Replace ALIAS with the alias of the HyperVault deployment.

    This command is a one-time operation per upgrade and does not restart the cluster. It ensures all nodes in the cluster agree on the same API version after the binary update.

    An API version bump is irreversible

    Bumping the API version is a one-way operation. Once the version is bumped, whether automatically or with mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api, you cannot roll it back, and downgrading the server binary is only possible if the API version has never been bumped. Running an older binary after a bump fails to start with an unsupported API version error.

    If you need to retain the ability to downgrade, set HYPERVAULT_API_AUTO_BUMP=off before upgrading so the version is not bumped automatically. To keep a bounded rollback window instead of disabling the bump, set HYPERVAULT_API_BUMP_BAKE_TIME to a duration. For recovery steps when a node fails to start due to an API version mismatch, see API version startup errors.

Upgrade HyperVault through binary replacement

You can download and manually replace the hypervault server binary on each of the host nodes in the cluster. You must then restart the cluster, such as by using mc admin service restart. This method targets clusters that do not rely on the DEB or RPM packages for installation.

  1. Download the HyperVault binary

    Download the latest stable HyperVault binary for Linux and copies it to /usr/local/bin. The command overwrites the existing hypervault binary at that path. Use the command appropriate for your host system CPU architecture.

    AMD64

    curl --retry 10 --progress-bar -L  https://dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/linux-amd64/hypervault
chmod +x ./hypervault

    ARM64

    curl --retry 10 --progress-bar -L  https://dl.min.io/hypervault/hypervault/release/linux-arm64/hypervault
chmod +x ./hypervault

  2. Replace the older binary

    Move and overwrite the existing binary using root permissions if necessary.

    sudo mv -f ./hypervault /usr/local/bin/hypervault

    Repeat for all nodes in the cluster.

  3. Restart the cluster

    Use the mc admin service restart command to restart the cluster, either all at once or with --rolling as shown in the DEB and RPM procedure above.

    Let mc admin service restart drive the restart rather than restarting nodes by hand. With --rolling, the command sequences the servers, gives each one a graceful wait period, and waits for each batch to report healthy before starting the next. Restarting nodes by hand does none of that, and clients connected to a node you restart receive connection errors unless a load balancer routes traffic away from it first. See Choose a restart mode.

    Monitor the status of the cluster using journalctl -uf hypervault. Once all nodes reach healthy status, you can further validate the upgrade using mc admin info.

  4. Upgrade HyperVault Client

    Upgrade your mc binary to match or closely follow the server release. You can use the mc update command to update the binary to the latest stable release:

    mc update

If some nodes are temporarily absent, the cluster tolerates their absence for up to one hour before committing the bump.

The cluster then holds the previous API version for that long after it is fully upgraded. The bump commits once all nodes have stayed online on the newer release for that duration. The bake time applies only while every node is online. If a node drops out, the cluster commits the bump once the remaining quorum has held the newer release for one hour, however long a bake time you configured, so a longer rollback window depends on keeping every node online for it. During the bake time, the cluster keeps writing data in the previous version’s format, so downgrading the server binary remains safe. The default is 0, which commits the bump immediately. A bake time applies only while automatic bumping is enabled. Features that require the new API version stay inactive until the bump commits, so a longer bake time also delays their availability.

    When automatic bumping is disabled, or when upgrading to a release earlier than RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, run the following command once all nodes are running the new version:

    mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api

    Replace ALIAS with the alias of the HyperVault deployment.

    This command is a one-time operation per upgrade and does not restart the cluster. It ensures all nodes in the cluster agree on the same API version after the binary update.

    An API version bump is irreversible

    Bumping the API version is a one-way operation. Once the version is bumped, whether automatically or with mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api, you cannot roll it back, and downgrading the server binary is only possible if the API version has never been bumped. Running an older binary after a bump fails to start with an unsupported API version error.

    If you need to retain the ability to downgrade, set HYPERVAULT_API_AUTO_BUMP=off before upgrading so the version is not bumped automatically. To keep a bounded rollback window instead of disabling the bump, set HYPERVAULT_API_BUMP_BAKE_TIME to a duration. For recovery steps when a node fails to start due to an API version mismatch, see API version startup errors.

Upgrade HyperVault using CLI commands

The mc admin update command updates the HyperVault binary on all hosts in the cluster and then restarts them. The command requires the following:

  • All host machines must have access to the internet such that they can resolve calls to the dl.min.io subdomain.

  • The system user and group hypervault-user have write access to the HyperVault hypervault binary, typically located at /usr/local/bin.

Use chown 775 hypervault-user:hypervault-user /usr/local/bin to set the appropriate permissions on all hosts prior to attempting to run the command.

For example, the following command updates a cluster with the alias PRODUCTION:

mc admin update PRODUCTION

The command provides a prompt to confirm the upgrade procedure. Follow the prompt to confirm and start the upgrade. Once completed, the cluster automatically restarts, with all hosts restarting at the same time.

To restart the hosts in sequence instead and keep the cluster serving requests, add --rolling with a graceful wait period:

mc admin update PRODUCTION --rolling 2m

A rolling update requires a load balancer in front of the cluster. See Choose a restart mode.

Use the mc admin info command to validate the HyperVault version used by the cluster post upgrade.

Bump the API version

By default, the bump happens immediately once all nodes are online and support the latest version. Download the MinIO AIStor binary Download the latest stable MinIO AIStor binary for Linux and copies it to /usr/local/bin. The command overwrites the existing minio binary at that path. Use the command appropriate for your host system CPU architecture. AMD64 curl --retry 10 --progress-bar -L https://dl.min.io/aistor/minio/release/linux-amd64/minio chmod +x ./minio ARM64 curl --retry 10 --progress-bar -L https://dl.min.io/aistor/minio/release/linux-arm64/minio chmod +x ./minio Replace the older binary Move and overwrite the existing binary using root permissions if necessary. sudo mv -f ./minio /usr/local/bin/minio Repeat for all nodes in the cluster. Restart the cluster Use the mc admin service restart command to restart the cluster, either all at once or with --rolling as shown in the DEB and RPM procedure above. Let mc admin service restart drive the restart rather than restarting nodes by hand. With --rolling, the command sequences the servers, gives each one a graceful wait period, and waits for each batch to report healthy before starting the next. Restarting nodes by hand does none of that, and clients connected to a node you restart receive connection errors unless a load balancer routes traffic away from it first. See Choose a restart mode. Monitor the status of the cluster using journalctl -uf minio. Once all nodes reach healthy status, you can further validate the upgrade using mc admin info. Upgrade AIStor Client Upgrade your mc binary to match or closely follow the server release. You can use the mc update command to update the binary to the latest stable release: mc update Bump the API version Starting with RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, the cluster leader automatically advances the cluster to the latest API version after a rolling upgrade that changes the API version. The cluster then holds the previous API version for that long after it is fully upgraded. The bump commits once all nodes have stayed online on the newer release for that duration. The bake time applies only while every node is online. If a node drops out, the cluster commits the bump once the remaining quorum has held the newer release for one hour, however long a bake time you configured, so a longer rollback window depends on keeping every node online for it. During the bake time, the cluster keeps writing data in the previous version’s format, so downgrading the server binary remains safe. The default is 0, which commits the bump immediately. A bake time applies only while automatic bumping is enabled. Features that require the new API version stay inactive until the bump commits, so a longer bake time also delays their availability.
