title: Upgrade HyperVault on Kubernetes in Airgapped Environments | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Upgrade HyperVault on Kubernetes in Airgapped Environments

Upgrade HyperVault Helm clusters in completely airgapped environments that have no direct internet access.

If your cluster has internet access, see:

  • Upgrade with Public Registries
  • Upgrade with Private Registry

Overview

HyperVault Helm upgrades involve updating two components:

  1. Operator Chart - Controls CustomResourceDefinitions and core operator resources
  2. Object Store Chart - Deploys and manages the HyperVault instances

In airgapped environments, prepare the artifacts on a system with internet access. Then transfer the container images and Helm charts to the airgapped environment.

The HyperVault Operator upgrades an object store one pod at a time, so the cluster keeps serving requests for the whole upgrade. Each pod finishes the requests it is already handling before it stops, up to the number of seconds set in rollingTimeoutSeconds, which defaults to 600. A request still running when that period expires is cut off, so raise the value if your workload has requests longer than ten minutes.

Clients connected to a pod that restarts do reconnect, and a load balancer sends them to a pod that is still running. Most S3 SDKs retry failed operations, so applications generally do not surface an error.

Upgrading to or from a release earlier than RELEASE.2025-12-20T04-58-37Z replaces every pod at once instead, which stops the cluster until the pods come back.

For how this compares with restarting every node at once, and how to choose between them on Linux, see Choose a restart mode.

Downgrades or rollbacks are not guaranteed due to potentially breaking changes in underlying resources like the HyperVault CustomResourceDefinition.

Prerequisites

Complete all standard upgrade prerequisites, then prepare the following for your airgapped environment:

  • Identify a system with internet access for downloading images and charts
  • Prepare a method to transfer artifacts to the airgapped environment, such as removable media or secure file transfer
  • Verify you have credentials and push access to your private container registry
  • Ensure your Kubernetes cluster has pull access configured for your private registry
  • Verify that image pull secrets exist in the hypervault namespace with valid credentials: 
    kubectl get secret -n hypervault private-repo-pull-secret
    If the secret does not exist or credentials have changed, recreate it before upgrading

Step 1. Prepare operator artifacts (external system)

Perform these steps on a system with internet access.

  1. Copy the operator image to your private registry.

    Use skopeo to copy the operator image:

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/operator:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

    Replace:

    • RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z with your target operator version
    • PRIVATE_REGISTRY with your private registry hostname

If your private registry is not accessible from this system, you can save the image as a tarball and transfer it:

skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker-archive:hypervault-operator-RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z.tar

Then transfer the tarball and load it into your private registry from within the airgapped environment.

  1. Download the operator Helm chart.

    Pull the updated Helm chart:

    helm pull hypervault/hypervault-operator

    This downloads a .tgz file (for example, hypervault-operator-5.4.0.tgz).

  2. Transfer to airgapped environment.

    Transfer the following to your airgapped environment:

    • The operator container image (either pushed to your registry or as a tarball)
    • The operator Helm chart .tgz file

Step 2: Deploy operator chart (airgapped system)

Perform these steps within your airgapped environment.

  1. Verify the existing installation.

    Check the health and status of the operator:

    kubectl get all -n hypervault

  2. Upgrade the operator.

    Choose one of the following methods based on how you store Helm charts in your airgapped environment:

    helm upgrade -n hypervault hypervault oci://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/helm-charts/hypervault-operator \
  --set license="eyJhbGciOiJFUzM4NCIsInR..." \
  -f hypervault-operator-values.yaml

    helm upgrade -n hypervault hypervault ./hypervault-operator-*.tgz \
  --set license="eyJhbGciOiJFUzM4NCIsInR..." \
  -f hypervault-operator-values.yaml

    Replace the license value with your decoded JWT token from SUBNET.

    Ensure your hypervault-operator-values.yaml file contains the repositories configuration pointing to your private registry. For example:

    repositories:
  hypervault:
    hostname: PRIVATE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY
    pathPrefix: hypervault/
    imagePullSecrets:
    - name: private-repo-pull-secret
  hypervault:
    hostname: PRIVATE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY
    pathPrefix: hypervault/
    imagePullSecrets:
    - name: private-repo-pull-secret

    Replace PRIVATE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY with the hostname of your private container registry (for example, registry.example.com or registry.example.com:5000).

    If you need to override specific image versions, add an images section:

    images:
  operator:
    repository: hypervault
    image: operator:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

  3. Validate the operator upgrade.

    Validate the installation by running the following command: 

    kubectl get all -n hypervault

    The output should show running pods similar to the following:

    NAME                                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
   pod/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f-hjbp5         1/1     Running   0          4m16s
   pod/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85-kmwlv   1/1     Running   0          4m16s
   
   NAME                            TYPE        CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)    AGE
   service/object-store-operator   ClusterIP   10.43.210.230   <none>        4221/TCP   4m16s
   
   NAME                                    READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
   deployment.apps/adminjob-operator       1/1     1            1           4m16s
   deployment.apps/object-store-operator   1/1     1            1           4m16s
   
   NAME                                               DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
   replicaset.apps/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f         1         1         1       4m16s
   replicaset.apps/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85   1         1         1       4m16s

Step 3: Prepare object store artifacts (external system)

Return to the system with internet access to prepare the object store artifacts.

  1. Copy the core object store images.

    Copy the main HyperVault images to your private registry:

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/hypervault:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/hypervault-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

    Replace:

    • RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z with your target version
    • PRIVATE_REGISTRY with your registry hostname

If your private registry is not accessible from this system, save the images as tarballs:

skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker-archive:hypervault-hypervault-RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z.tar

skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker-archive:hypervault-hypervault-sidecar-RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z.tar

  1. Copy optional images.

    If you use additional features, copy those images as well:

    # KES (Key Encryption Service)
skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/kes:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/kes:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

# HyperVault Client (mc)
skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/mc:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/mc:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

# AI Hub (if using AI features)
skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/aihub:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/aihub:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

# Prompt (if using AI features)
skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/prompt:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/prompt:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

# WARP (benchmarking tool)
skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/warp:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/warp:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

  2. Download the object store Helm chart.

    Pull the updated Helm chart:

    helm pull hypervault/hypervault-objectstore

    This downloads a .tgz file (for example, hypervault-objectstore-6.0.5.tgz).

  3. Transfer to airgapped environment.

    Transfer the following to your airgapped environment:

    • All object store container images (either pushed to your registry or as tarballs)
    • The object store Helm chart .tgz file

Step 4: Deploy object store chart (airgapped system)

Return to your airgapped environment to deploy the object store chart update.

  1. Verify the existing installation.

    Check the health and status of your object store:

    kubectl get all -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE

    Replace OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE with your object store’s namespace.

  2. Upgrade the object store chart.

    Choose one of the following methods based on how you store Helm charts:

    helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME oci://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/helm-charts/hypervault-objectstore \
  -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

    helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME ./hypervault-objectstore-*.tgz \
  -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

    Replace:

    • OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE with your object store’s namespace
    • OBJECT-STORE-NAME with your object store’s Helm release name
    • hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml with the path to your values file

You must pass in your existing chart values file to ensure your customized settings are preserved during the upgrade.

Your values file should already contain the repositories configuration from your initial installation. The Helm chart automatically references images from these repositories. For example:

objectStore:
  name: primary-object-store
  pools:
  - name: pool-0
    servers: 8
    volumesPerServer: 8
    size: 2Ti
  services:
    hypervault:
      serviceType: NodePort
      nodePort: 31000

The operator uses the repositories configuration from the operator values file to determine where to pull images. If you need to override specific image versions in the object store cluster, you can add image overrides:

objectStore:
  image:
    repository: hypervault  # References repositories.hypervault
    image: hypervault:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z
  sidecar:
    image:
      repository: hypervault  # References repositories.hypervault
      image: hypervault-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

  1. Validate the object store upgrade.

    Confirm the object store pods are running with the new version:

    kubectl get all -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE

    Check the pods are ready and the cluster is healthy.

  2. Bump the API version.

    Starting with RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, the cluster leader automatically advances the cluster to the latest API version after a rolling upgrade that changes the API version. By default, the bump happens immediately once all nodes are online and support the latest version. If some nodes are temporarily absent, the cluster tolerates their absence for up to one hour before committing the bump.

    Automatic bumping is enabled by default. To disable it and manage the API version manually, set HYPERVAULT_API_AUTO_BUMP=off on all nodes before upgrading.

    Starting with RELEASE.2026-07-24T16-43-31Z, you can delay the bump instead of disabling it. Set HYPERVAULT_API_BUMP_BAKE_TIME on all nodes to a duration, for example 1h, to configure a bake time. The cluster then holds the previous API version for that long after it is fully upgraded. The bump commits once all nodes have stayed online on the newer release for that duration. The bake time applies only while every node is online. If a node drops out, the cluster commits the bump once the remaining quorum has held the newer release for one hour, however long a bake time you configured, so a longer rollback window depends on keeping every node online for it. During the bake time, the cluster keeps writing data in the previous version’s format, so downgrading the server binary remains safe. The default is 0, which commits the bump immediately. A bake time applies only while automatic bumping is enabled. Features that require the new API version stay inactive until the bump commits, so a longer bake time also delays their availability.

    When automatic bumping is disabled, or when upgrading to a release earlier than RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, run the following command once all nodes are running the new version:

    mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api

    Replace ALIAS with the alias of the HyperVault deployment.

    This command is a one-time operation per upgrade and does not restart the cluster. It ensures all nodes in the cluster agree on the same API version after the binary update.

    An API version bump is irreversible

    Bumping the API version is a one-way operation. Once the version is bumped, whether automatically or with mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api, you cannot roll it back, and downgrading the server binary is only possible if the API version has never been bumped. Running an older binary after a bump fails to start with an unsupported API version error.

    If you need to retain the ability to downgrade, set HYPERVAULT_API_AUTO_BUMP=off before upgrading so the version is not bumped automatically. To keep a bounded rollback window instead of disabling the bump, set HYPERVAULT_API_BUMP_BAKE_TIME to a duration. For recovery steps when a node fails to start due to an API version mismatch, see API version startup errors.

Upgrade only the object store image

If you want to update only the HyperVault binary version without upgrading the chart itself, you can specify a new image tag. This approach keeps your existing chart version but updates the running software.

  1. Prepare the image (External System).

    On a system with internet access, copy the new image version:

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault:RELEASE.2025-05-30T11-03-39Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/hypervault:RELEASE.2025-05-30T11-03-39Z

    Or save as a tarball for transfer:

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault:RELEASE.2025-05-30T11-03-39Z \
  docker-archive:hypervault-hypervault-RELEASE.2025-05-30T11-03-39Z.tar

    Replace the tag with your target release version.

    Transfer the image to your airgapped environment and load it into your private registry if using tarballs.

  2. Update the values file (Airgapped System).

    Edit your hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml file and update the image tag:

    objectStore:
  image:
    repository: PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/hypervault
    tag: RELEASE.2025-05-30T11-03-39Z

  3. Deploy the image update.

    Apply the updated configuration using the same method you used for the initial installation:

    helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME oci://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/helm-charts/hypervault-objectstore \
  -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

    helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME private-hypervault/hypervault-objectstore \
  -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

    helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME ./hypervault-objectstore-*.tgz \
  -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

  4. Validate the cluster.

    Verify the pods are running with the new image:

    kubectl get pods -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.containers[?(@.name=="hypervault")].image}'

    This command displays the image versions running in your pods. Confirm they reference your private registry with the new tag.

  5. Bump the API version.

    Starting with RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, the cluster leader automatically advances the cluster to the latest API version after a rolling upgrade that changes the API version. By default, the bump happens immediately once all nodes are online and support the latest version. If some nodes are temporarily absent, the cluster tolerates their absence for up to one hour before committing the bump.

    Replace ALIAS with the alias of the HyperVault deployment.

Downgrades or rollbacks are not guaranteed due to potentially breaking changes in underlying resources like the MinIO AIStor CustomResourceDefinition. Prerequisites Complete all standard upgrade prerequisites, then prepare the following for your airgapped environment: Identify a system with internet access for downloading images and charts Prepare a method to transfer artifacts to the airgapped environment, such as removable media or secure file transfer Verify you have credentials and push access to your private container registry Ensure your Kubernetes cluster has pull access configured for your private registry Verify that image pull secrets exist in the aistor namespace with valid credentials: kubectl get secret -n aistor private-repo-pull-secret If the secret does not exist or credentials have changed, recreate it before upgrading Step 1. Prepare operator artifacts (external system) Perform these steps on a system with internet access. Copy the operator image to your private registry. Use skopeo to copy the operator image: skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \ docker://quay.io/minio/aistor/operator:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \ docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/aistor/operator:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z Replace: RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z with your target operator version PRIVATE_REGISTRY with your private registry hostname If your private registry is not accessible from this system, you can save the image as a tarball and transfer it: skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \ docker://quay.io/minio/aistor/operator:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \ docker-archive:aistor-operator-RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z.tar Then transfer the tarball and load it into your private registry from within the airgapped environment. Download the operator Helm chart. Pull the updated Helm chart: helm pull minio/aistor-operator This downloads a .tgz file (for example, aistor-operator-5.4.0.tgz). Transfer to airgapped environment. Transfer the following to your airgapped environment: The operator container image (either pushed to your registry or as a tarball) The operator Helm chart .tgz file Step 2: Deploy operator chart (airgapped system) Perform these steps within your airgapped environment. Verify the existing installation. Check the health and status of the operator: kubectl get all -n aistor Upgrade the operator. Choose one of the following methods based on how you store Helm charts in your airgapped environment: OCI Registry helm upgrade -n aistor aistor oci://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/helm-charts/aistor-operator \ --set license="eyJhbGciOiJFUzM4NCIsInR..." \ -f aistor-operator-values.yaml Local Chart File helm upgrade -n aistor aistor ./aistor-operator-*.tgz \ --set license="eyJhbGciOiJFUzM4NCIsInR..." \ -f aistor-operator-values.yaml Replace the license value with your decoded JWT token from SUBNET. Ensure your aistor-operator-values.yaml file contains the repositories configuration pointing to your private registry. For example: repositories: aistor: hostname: PRIVATE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY pathPrefix: aistor/ imagePullSecrets: - name: private-repo-pull-secret minio: hostname: PRIVATE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY pathPrefix: minio/ imagePullSecrets: - name: private-repo-pull-secret Replace PRIVATE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY with the hostname of your private container registry (for example, registry.example.com or registry.example.com:5000). If you need to override specific image versions, add an images section: images: operator: repository: aistor image: operator:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z Validate the operator upgrade. Validate the installation by running the following command: kubectl get all -n aistor The output should show running pods similar to the following: NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE pod/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f-hjbp5 1/1 Running 0 4m16s pod/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85-kmwlv 1/1 Running 0 4m16s NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) AGE service/object-store-operator ClusterIP 10.43.210.230 <none> 4221/TCP 4m16s NAME READY UP-TO-DATE AVAILABLE AGE deployment.apps/adminjob-operator 1/1 1 1 4m16s deployment.apps/object-store-operator 1/1 1 1 4m16s NAME DESIRED CURRENT READY AGE replicaset.apps/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f 1 1 1 4m16s replicaset.apps/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85 1 1 1 4m16s Step 3: Prepare object store artifacts (external system) Return to the system with internet access to prepare the object store artifacts. Copy the core object store images. Copy the main MinIO AIStor images to your private registry: skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \ docker://quay.io/minio/aistor/minio:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \ docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/aistor/minio:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \ docker://quay.io/minio/aistor/minio-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \ docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/aistor/minio-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z Replace: RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z with your target version PRIVATE_REGISTRY with your registry hostname If your private registry is not accessible from this system, save the images as tarballs: skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \ docker://quay.io/minio/aistor/minio:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \ docker-archive:aistor-minio-RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z.tar skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \ docker://quay.io/minio/aistor/minio-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \ docker-archive:aistor-minio-sidecar-RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z.tar Copy optional images. Verify the existing installation. Check the health and status of your object store: kubectl get all -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE Replace OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE with your object store’s namespace. Upgrade the object store chart. Choose one of the following methods based on how you store Helm charts: OCI Registry helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME oci://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/helm-charts/aistor-objectstore \ -f aistor-objectstore-values.yaml Local Chart File helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME ./aistor-objectstore-*.tgz \ -f aistor-objectstore-values.yaml Replace: OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE with your object store’s namespace OBJECT-STORE-NAME with your object store’s Helm release name aistor-objectstore-values.yaml with the path to your values file You must pass in your existing chart values file to ensure your customized settings are preserved during the upgrade. Your values file should already contain the repositories configuration from your initial installation. The Helm chart automatically references images from these repositories. For example: objectStore: name: primary-object-store pools: - name: pool-0 servers: 8 volumesPerServer: 8 size: 2Ti services: minio: serviceType: NodePort nodePort: 31000 The operator uses the repositories configuration from the operator values file to determine where to pull images. If you need to override specific image versions in the object store cluster, you can add image overrides: objectStore: image: repository: aistor # References repositories.aistor image: minio:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z sidecar: image: repository: aistor # References repositories.aistor image: minio-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z Validate the object store upgrade. Confirm the object store pods are running with the new version: kubectl get all -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE Check the pods are ready and the cluster is healthy. Bump the API version. Starting with RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, the cluster leader automatically advances the cluster to the latest API version after a rolling upgrade that changes the API version. By default, the bump happens immediately once all nodes are online and support the latest version. If some nodes are temporarily absent, the cluster tolerates their absence for up to one hour before committing the bump. Automatic bumping is enabled by default. To disable it and manage the API version manually, set MINIO_API_AUTO_BUMP=off on all nodes before upgrading. Starting with RELEASE.2026-07-24T16-43-31Z, you can delay the bump instead of disabling it. Set MINIO_API_BUMP_BAKE_TIME on all nodes to a duration, for example 1h, to configure a bake time. The cluster then holds the previous API version for that long after it is fully upgraded. The bump commits once all nodes have stayed online on the newer release for that duration. The bake time applies only while every node is online. If a node drops out, the cluster commits the bump once the remaining quorum has held the newer release for one hour, however long a bake time you configured, so a longer rollback window depends on keeping every node online for it. During the bake time, the cluster keeps writing data in the previous version’s format, so downgrading the server binary remains safe. The default is 0, which commits the bump immediately. A bake time applies only while automatic bumping is enabled. Features that require the new API version stay inactive until the bump commits, so a longer bake time also delays their availability. When automatic bumping is disabled, or when upgrading to a release earlier than RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, run the following command once all nodes are running the new version: mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api Replace ALIAS with the alias of the MinIO AIStor deployment. This command is a one-time operation per upgrade and does not restart the cluster. It ensures all nodes in the cluster agree on the same API version after the binary update. An API version bump is irreversible Bumping the API version is a one-way operation. Once the version is bumped, whether automatically or with mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api, you cannot roll it back, and downgrading the server binary is only possible if the API version has never been bumped. Running an older binary after a bump fails to start with an unsupported API version error. If you need to retain the ability to downgrade, set MINIO_API_AUTO_BUMP=off before upgrading so the version is not bumped automatically. To keep a bounded rollback window instead of disabling the bump, set MINIO_API_BUMP_BAKE_TIME to a duration. Transfer the image to your airgapped environment and load it into your private registry if using tarballs. Update the values file (Airgapped System). Edit your aistor-objectstore-values.yaml file and update the image tag: objectStore: image: repository: PRIVATE_REGISTRY/aistor/minio tag: RELEASE.2025-05-30T11-03-39Z Deploy the image update. Apply the updated configuration using the same method you used for the initial installation: OCI Registry helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME oci://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/helm-charts/aistor-objectstore \ -f aistor-objectstore-values.yaml HTTP Repository helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME private-minio/aistor-objectstore \ -f aistor-objectstore-values.yaml Local Chart File helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME ./aistor-objectstore-*.tgz \ -f aistor-objectstore-values.yaml Validate the cluster. Verify the pods are running with the new image: kubectl get pods -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.containers[?(@.name=="minio")].image}' This command displays the image versions running in your pods. Confirm they reference your private registry with the new tag. Bump the API version. Starting with RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, the cluster leader automatically advances the cluster to the latest API version after a rolling upgrade that changes the API version. A bake time applies only while automatic bumping is enabled. Features that require the new API version stay inactive until the bump commits, so a longer bake time also delays their availability. title: Upgrade HyperVault on Kubernetes with Private Registry | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Upgrade HyperVault on Kubernetes with Private Registry

Upgrade HyperVault Helm clusters that use a private container registry but have internet access to helm.min.io for chart updates.

If your cluster uses public registries or is in an airgapped environment, see:

  • Upgrade with Public Registries
  • Upgrade in Airgapped Environment

Overview

HyperVault Helm upgrades involve updating two components:

  1. Operator Chart - Controls CustomResourceDefinitions and core operator resources
  2. Object Store Chart - Deploys and manages the HyperVault instances

When you use a private registry, copy the container images to that registry before you deploy the chart updates.

The HyperVault Operator upgrades an object store one pod at a time, so the cluster keeps serving requests for the whole upgrade. Each pod finishes the requests it is already handling before it stops, up to the number of seconds set in rollingTimeoutSeconds, which defaults to 600. A request still running when that period expires is cut off, so raise the value if your workload has requests longer than ten minutes.

Clients connected to a pod that restarts do reconnect, and a load balancer sends them to a pod that is still running. Most S3 SDKs retry failed operations, so applications generally do not surface an error.

Upgrading to or from a release earlier than RELEASE.2025-12-20T04-58-37Z replaces every pod at once instead, which stops the cluster until the pods come back.

For how this compares with restarting every node at once, and how to choose between them on Linux, see Choose a restart mode.

Prerequisites

Complete all standard upgrade prerequisites, then prepare the following for your private registry environment:

  • Verify you have network access to helm.min.io and quay.io
  • Verify you have credentials and push access to your private container registry
  • Ensure your Kubernetes cluster has pull access configured for your private registry
  • Verify that image pull secrets exist in the hypervault namespace with valid credentials: 
    kubectl get secret -n hypervault private-repo-pull-secret
    If the secret does not exist or credentials have changed, recreate it before upgrading

Step 1. Copy operator image to private registry

Before upgrading the operator chart, copy the new operator image to your private registry.

  1. Copy the operator image.

    Use skopeo or a similar tool to copy the image:

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/operator:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

    Replace:

    • RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z with your target operator version
    • PRIVATE_REGISTRY with your registry hostname

Step 2: Upgrade the operator chart

The operator chart provides the core resources for deploying HyperVault onto Kubernetes.

Downgrades or rollbacks are not guaranteed due to potentially breaking changes in underlying resources like the HyperVault CustomResourceDefinition.

  1. Verify the existing installation.

    Check the health and status of the operator:

    kubectl get all -n hypervault

  2. Update and upgrade the operator.

    Update the Helm repository:

    helm repo update hypervault

    Upgrade the operator chart with your private registry configuration:

    helm upgrade -n hypervault hypervault hypervault/hypervault-operator \
  --set license="eyJhbGciOiJFUzM4NCIsInR..." \
  -f hypervault-operator-values.yaml

    Replace the license value with your decoded JWT token from SUBNET.

    Ensure your hypervault-operator-values.yaml file contains the repositories configuration pointing to your private registry. For example:

    repositories:
  hypervault:
    hostname: PRIVATE_REGISTRY
    pathPrefix: hypervault/
    imagePullSecrets:
    - name: private-repo-pull-secret
  hypervault:
    hostname: PRIVATE_REGISTRY
    pathPrefix: hypervault/
    imagePullSecrets:
    - name: private-repo-pull-secret

    Replace PRIVATE_REGISTRY with the hostname of your private container registry (for example, registry.example.com or registry.example.com:5000).

    If you need to override specific image versions, add an images section:

    images:
  operator:
    repository: hypervault
    image: operator:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

  3. Validate the installation by running the following command: 

    kubectl get all -n hypervault

    The output should show running pods similar to the following:

    NAME                                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f-hjbp5         1/1     Running   0          4m16s
pod/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85-kmwlv   1/1     Running   0          4m16s

NAME                            TYPE        CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)    AGE
service/object-store-operator   ClusterIP   10.43.210.230   <none>        4221/TCP   4m16s

NAME                                    READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
deployment.apps/adminjob-operator       1/1     1            1           4m16s
deployment.apps/object-store-operator   1/1     1            1           4m16s

NAME                                               DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
replicaset.apps/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f         1         1         1       4m16s
replicaset.apps/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85   1         1         1       4m16s

Step 3: Copy object store images to private registry

Before upgrading the object store chart, copy the required images to your private registry.

  1. Copy the core object store images.

    Copy the main HyperVault images:

    skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/hypervault:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/hypervault-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

    Replace:

    • RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z with your target version
    • PRIVATE_REGISTRY with your registry hostname

  2. Copy optional images.

    If you use additional features, copy those images as well:

    # KES (Key Encryption Service)
skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/kes:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/kes:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

# HyperVault Client (mc)
skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/mc:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/mc:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

# AI Hub (if using AI features)
skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/aihub:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/aihub:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

# Prompt (if using AI features)
skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/prompt:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/prompt:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

# WARP (benchmarking tool)
skopeo copy --override-os linux --override-arch amd64 \
  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/warp:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/warp:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

Step 4: Upgrade the object store chart

The object store chart deploys and manages your HyperVault instances.

Downgrades or rollbacks are not guaranteed due to potentially breaking changes in the HyperVault.

  1. Verify the existing installation.

    Check the health and status of your object store:

    kubectl get all -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE

    Replace OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE with your object store’s namespace.

  2. Update the Helm repository.

    Update the Helm repository to get the latest chart version:

    helm repo update hypervault

  3. Upgrade the object store chart.

    Use helm upgrade to deploy the updated chart:

    helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME hypervault/hypervault-objectstore \
  -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

    Replace:

    • OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE with your object store’s namespace
    • OBJECT-STORE-NAME with your object store’s Helm release name
    • hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml with the path to your values file

You must pass in your existing chart values file to ensure your customized settings are preserved during the upgrade.

Your values file should already contain the repositories configuration from your initial installation. The Helm chart automatically references images from these repositories. For example:

objectStore:
  name: primary-object-store
  pools:
  - name: pool-0
    servers: 8
    volumesPerServer: 8
    size: 2Ti
  services:
    hypervault:
      serviceType: NodePort
      nodePort: 31000

The operator uses the repositories configuration from the operator values file to determine where to pull images. If you need to override specific image versions in the object store cluster, you can add image overrides:

objectStore:
  image:
    repository: hypervault  # References repositories.hypervault
    image: hypervault:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z
  sidecar:
    image:
      repository: hypervault  # References repositories.hypervault
      image: hypervault-sidecar:RELEASE.2025-XX-XXT00-00-00Z

  1. Validate the object store upgrade.

    Confirm the object store pods are running with the new version:

    kubectl get all -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE

    Check the pods are ready and the cluster is healthy.

  2. Bump the API version.

    Starting with RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, the cluster leader automatically advances the cluster to the latest API version after a rolling upgrade that changes the API version. By default, the bump happens immediately once all nodes are online and support the latest version. If some nodes are temporarily absent, the cluster tolerates their absence for up to one hour before committing the bump.

    Automatic bumping is enabled by default. To disable it and manage the API version manually, set HYPERVAULT_API_AUTO_BUMP=off on all nodes before upgrading.

    Starting with RELEASE.2026-07-24T16-43-31Z, you can delay the bump instead of disabling it. Set HYPERVAULT_API_BUMP_BAKE_TIME on all nodes to a duration, for example 1h, to configure a bake time. The cluster then holds the previous API version for that long after it is fully upgraded. The bump commits once all nodes have stayed online on the newer release for that duration. The bake time applies only while every node is online. If a node drops out, the cluster commits the bump once the remaining quorum has held the newer release for one hour, however long a bake time you configured, so a longer rollback window depends on keeping every node online for it. During the bake time, the cluster keeps writing data in the previous version’s format, so downgrading the server binary remains safe. The default is 0, which commits the bump immediately. A bake time applies only while automatic bumping is enabled. Features that require the new API version stay inactive until the bump commits, so a longer bake time also delays their availability.

    When automatic bumping is disabled, or when upgrading to a release earlier than RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, run the following command once all nodes are running the new version:

    mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api

    Replace ALIAS with the alias of the HyperVault deployment.

    This command is a one-time operation per upgrade and does not restart the cluster. It ensures all nodes in the cluster agree on the same API version after the binary update.

    An API version bump is irreversible

    Bumping the API version is a one-way operation. Once the version is bumped, whether automatically or with mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api, you cannot roll it back, and downgrading the server binary is only possible if the API version has never been bumped. Running an older binary after a bump fails to start with an unsupported API version error.

To keep a bounded rollback window instead of disabling the bump, set HYPERVAULT_API_BUMP_BAKE_TIME to a duration. For recovery steps when a node fails to start due to an API version mismatch, see API version startup errors.

If you want to update only the HyperVault binary version without upgrading the chart itself, you can specify a new image tag. This approach keeps your existing chart version but updates the running software.

    Copy the new image version to your private registry:

  docker://quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault:RELEASE.2025-05-30T11-03-39Z \
  docker://PRIVATE_REGISTRY/hypervault/hypervault:RELEASE.2025-05-30T11-03-39Z

    Replace the tag with your target release version and PRIVATE_REGISTRY with your registry hostname.

  2. Update the values file.

    Edit your hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml file and update the image tag:

    tag: RELEASE.2025-05-30T11-03-39Z

    Apply the updated configuration:

    This command displays the image versions running in your pods. Confirm they reference your private registry with the new tag.

  5. Bump the API version.

    Starting with RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, the cluster leader automatically advances the cluster to the latest API version after a rolling upgrade that changes the API version. By default, the bump happens immediately once all nodes are online and support the latest version. If some nodes are temporarily absent, the cluster tolerates their absence for up to one hour before committing the bump.

The cluster then holds the previous API version for that long after it is fully upgraded. The bump commits once all nodes have stayed online on the newer release for that duration. The bake time applies only while every node is online. If a node drops out, the cluster commits the bump once the remaining quorum has held the newer release for one hour, however long a bake time you configured, so a longer rollback window depends on keeping every node online for it. During the bake time, the cluster keeps writing data in the previous version’s format, so downgrading the server binary remains safe. The default is 0, which commits the bump immediately. A bake time applies only while automatic bumping is enabled. Features that require the new API version stay inactive until the bump commits, so a longer bake time also delays their availability.

    When automatic bumping is disabled, or when upgrading to a release earlier than RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, run the following command once all nodes are running the new version:

    mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api

    Replace ALIAS with the alias of the HyperVault deployment.

    This command is a one-time operation per upgrade and does not restart the cluster. It ensures all nodes in the cluster agree on the same API version after the binary update.

    An API version bump is irreversible

    Bumping the API version is a one-way operation. Once the version is bumped, whether automatically or with mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api, you cannot roll it back, and downgrading the server binary is only possible if the API version has never been bumped. title: Upgrade HyperVault on Kubernetes with Public Registries | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Upgrade HyperVault on Kubernetes with Public Registries

Upgrade HyperVault Helm clusters that use public registries and have direct internet access to helm.min.io and quay.io.

If your cluster uses a private container registry or is in an airgapped environment, see:

  • Upgrade with Private Registry
  • Upgrade in Airgapped Environment

Overview

HyperVault Helm upgrades involve updating two components:

  1. Operator Chart - Controls CustomResourceDefinitions and core operator resources
  2. Object Store Chart - Deploys and manages the HyperVault instances

You can upgrade both components together or independently.

The HyperVault Operator upgrades an object store one pod at a time, so the cluster keeps serving requests for the whole upgrade. Each pod finishes the requests it is already handling before it stops, up to the number of seconds set in rollingTimeoutSeconds, which defaults to 600. A request still running when that period expires is cut off, so raise the value if your workload has requests longer than ten minutes.

Clients connected to a pod that restarts do reconnect, and a load balancer sends them to a pod that is still running. Most S3 SDKs retry failed operations, so applications generally do not surface an error.

Upgrading to or from a release earlier than RELEASE.2025-12-20T04-58-37Z replaces every pod at once instead, which stops the cluster until the pods come back.

For how this compares with restarting every node at once, and how to choose between them on Linux, see Choose a restart mode.

Prerequisites

Complete all standard upgrade prerequisites, then verify you have network access to helm.min.io and quay.io.

Step 1: Upgrade the operator chart

The operator chart provides the core resources for deploying HyperVault onto Kubernetes.

The operator chart was renamed from hypervault-objectstore-operator to hypervault-operator in chart version 5.2.0. Both names refer to the same chart.

If your release still points at hypervault-objectstore-operator, upgrade the release to the hypervault/hypervault-operator chart with the steps below. Keep the release name and namespace you already use, in place of hypervault in the example command. Helm upgrades the release in place, so you do not need to uninstall the release or create a new one under a different name.

  1. Verify the existing installation.

    Check the health and status of the operator:

    kubectl get all -n hypervault

  2. Update and upgrade the operator.

    Update the Helm repository:

    helm repo update hypervault

    Upgrade the operator chart:

    helm upgrade -n hypervault hypervault hypervault/hypervault-operator \
  --set license="eyJhbGciOiJFUzM4NCIsInR..."

    Replace the license value with your decoded JWT token from SUBNET.

  3. Validate the installation by running the following command: 

    kubectl get all -n hypervault

    The output should show running pods similar to the following:

    NAME                                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f-hjbp5         1/1     Running   0          4m16s
pod/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85-kmwlv   1/1     Running   0          4m16s

NAME                            TYPE        CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)    AGE
service/object-store-operator   ClusterIP   10.43.210.230   <none>        4221/TCP   4m16s

NAME                                    READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
deployment.apps/adminjob-operator       1/1     1            1           4m16s
deployment.apps/object-store-operator   1/1     1            1           4m16s

NAME                                               DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
replicaset.apps/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f         1         1         1       4m16s
replicaset.apps/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85   1         1         1       4m16s

Step 2: Upgrade the object store chart

The object store chart deploys and manages your HyperVault instances.

Downgrades or rollbacks are not guaranteed due to potentially breaking changes in the HyperVault.

  1. Verify the existing installation.

    Check the health and status of your object store:

    kubectl get all -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE

    Replace OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE with your object store’s namespace.

  2. Update the Helm repository.

    Update the Helm repository to get the latest chart version:

    helm repo update hypervault

  3. Upgrade the object store chart.

    Use helm upgrade to deploy the updated chart:

    helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME hypervault/hypervault-objectstore \
  -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

    Replace:

    • OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE with your object store’s namespace
    • OBJECT-STORE-NAME with your object store’s Helm release name
    • hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml with the path to your values file
You must pass in your existing chart values file to ensure your customized settings are preserved during the upgrade.

  1. Validate the object store upgrade.

    Confirm the object store pods are running with the new version:

    kubectl get all -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE

    Check the pods are ready and the cluster is healthy.

  image:
    repository: quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault

    Replace the tag with your target release version.

    Apply the updated configuration:

    helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME hypervault/hypervault-objectstore \
  -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

If a node drops out, the cluster commits the bump once the remaining quorum has held the newer release for one hour, however long a bake time you configured, so a longer rollback window depends on keeping every node online for it. During the bake time, the cluster keeps writing data in the previous version’s format, so downgrading the server binary remains safe. The default is 0, which commits the bump immediately. A bake time applies only while automatic bumping is enabled. Features that require the new API version stay inactive until the bump commits, so a longer bake time also delays their availability.

    When automatic bumping is disabled, or when upgrading to a release earlier than RELEASE.2026-04-11T03-20-12Z, run the following command once all nodes are running the new version:

    mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api

    Replace ALIAS with the alias of the HyperVault deployment.

    This command is a one-time operation per upgrade and does not restart the cluster. It ensures all nodes in the cluster agree on the same API version after the binary update.

    An API version bump is irreversible

    Bumping the API version is a one-way operation. Once the version is bumped, whether automatically or with mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api, you cannot roll it back, and downgrading the server binary is only possible if the API version has never been bumped. Running an older binary after a bump fails to start with an unsupported API version error.

    If you need to retain the ability to downgrade, set HYPERVAULT_API_AUTO_BUMP=off before upgrading so the version is not bumped automatically. To keep a bounded rollback window instead of disabling the bump, set HYPERVAULT_API_BUMP_BAKE_TIME to a duration. For recovery steps when a node fails to start due to an API version mismatch, see API version startup errors.
text: Upgrade MinIO AIStor on Kubernetes with Public Registries Upgrade MinIO AIStor Helm clusters that use public registries and have direct internet access to helm.min.io and quay.io. If your cluster uses a private container registry or is in an airgapped environment, see: Upgrade with Private Registry Upgrade in Airgapped Environment Overview MinIO AIStor Helm upgrades involve updating two components: Operator Chart - Controls CustomResourceDefinitions and core operator resources Object Store Chart - Deploys and manages the MinIO AIStor instances You can upgrade both components together or independently. The AIStor Operator upgrades an object store one pod at a time, so the cluster keeps serving requests for the whole upgrade. Each pod finishes the requests it is already handling before it stops, up to the number of seconds set in rollingTimeoutSeconds, which defaults to 600. A request still running when that period expires is cut off, so raise the value if your workload has requests longer than ten minutes. Clients connected to a pod that restarts do reconnect, and a load balancer sends them to a pod that is still running. Most S3 SDKs retry failed operations, so applications generally do not surface an error. Upgrading to or from a release earlier than RELEASE.2025-12-20T04-58-37Z replaces every pod at once instead, which stops the cluster until the pods come back. For how this compares with restarting every node at once, and how to choose between them on Linux, see Choose a restart mode. Prerequisites Complete all standard upgrade prerequisites, then verify you have network access to helm.min.io and quay.io. Step 1: Upgrade the operator chart The operator chart provides the core resources for deploying MinIO AIStor onto Kubernetes. The operator chart was renamed from aistor-objectstore-operator to aistor-operator in chart version 5.2.0. Both names refer to the same chart. If your release still points at aistor-objectstore-operator, upgrade the release to the minio/aistor-operator chart with the steps below. Keep the release name and namespace you already use, in place of aistor in the example command. Helm upgrades the release in place, so you do not need to uninstall the release or create a new one under a different name. Verify the existing installation. Check the health and status of the operator: kubectl get all -n aistor Update and upgrade the operator. Update the Helm repository: helm repo update minio Upgrade the operator chart: helm upgrade -n aistor aistor minio/aistor-operator \ --set license="eyJhbGciOiJFUzM4NCIsInR..." Replace the license value with your decoded JWT token from SUBNET. Validate the installation by running the following command: kubectl get all -n aistor The output should show running pods similar to the following: NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE pod/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f-hjbp5 1/1 Running 0 4m16s pod/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85-kmwlv 1/1 Running 0 4m16s NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) AGE service/object-store-operator ClusterIP 10.43.210.230 <none> 4221/TCP 4m16s NAME READY UP-TO-DATE AVAILABLE AGE deployment.apps/adminjob-operator 1/1 1 1 4m16s deployment.apps/object-store-operator 1/1 1 1 4m16s NAME DESIRED CURRENT READY AGE replicaset.apps/adminjob-operator-cfc97d9f 1 1 1 4m16s replicaset.apps/object-store-operator-78c9f84b85 1 1 1 4m16s Step 2: Upgrade the object store chart The object store chart deploys and manages your MinIO AIStor instances. Downgrades or rollbacks are not guaranteed due to potentially breaking changes in the MinIO AIStor. Verify the existing installation. Check the health and status of your object store: kubectl get all -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE Replace OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE with your object store’s namespace. Update the Helm repository. Update the Helm repository to get the latest chart version: helm repo update minio Upgrade the object store chart. Use helm upgrade to deploy the updated chart: helm upgrade -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE OBJECT-STORE-NAME minio/aistor-objectstore \ -f aistor-objectstore-values.yaml Replace: OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE with your object store’s namespace OBJECT-STORE-NAME with your object store’s Helm release name aistor-objectstore-values.yaml with the path to your values file You must pass in your existing chart values file to ensure your customized settings are preserved during the upgrade. Validate the object store upgrade. Confirm the object store pods are running with the new version: kubectl get all -n OBJECT-STORE-NAMESPACE Check the pods are ready and the cluster is healthy. By default, the bump happens immediately once all nodes are online and support the latest version. If some nodes are temporarily absent, the cluster tolerates their absence for up to one hour before committing the bump. Automatic bumping is enabled by default. To disable it and manage the API version manually, set MINIO_API_AUTO_BUMP=off on all nodes before upgrading. Starting with RELEASE.2026-07-24T16-43-31Z, you can delay the bump instead of disabling it. Set MINIO_API_BUMP_BAKE_TIME on all nodes to a duration, for example 1h, to configure a bake time. The cluster then holds the previous API version for that long after it is fully upgraded. The bump commits once all nodes have stayed online on the newer release for that duration. The bake time applies only while every node is online. If a node drops out, the cluster commits the bump once the remaining quorum has held the newer release for one hour, however long a bake time you configured, so a longer rollback window depends on keeping every node online for it. During the bake time, the cluster keeps writing data in the previous version’s format, so downgrading the server binary remains safe. The default is 0, which commits the bump immediately. A bake time applies only while automatic bumping is enabled. Features that require the new API version stay inactive until the bump commits, so a longer bake time also delays their availability. An API version bump is irreversible Bumping the API version is a one-way operation. Once the version is bumped, whether automatically or with mc admin update ALIAS --bump-api, you cannot roll it back, and downgrading the server binary is only possible if the API version has never been bumped. title: HyperVault Tables | HyperVault Documentation
html:
HyperVault Tables

The following example creates an HyperVault Tables warehouse and performs basic table operations with the HyperVault Client and PyIceberg, a lightweight Python API for interacting with Iceberg Tables. You use the client to create the needed resources and Python code to insert and query data using the HyperVault Tables API.

You can also call the HyperVault Tables API directly, instead of working with the HyperVault client commands. See the HyperVault Tables API Reference for more information.

To connect query and analytics engines such as Spark, Trino, Starburst, or Dremio, see Connecting query engines to HyperVault Tables, which includes a supported-engine compatibility matrix and complete catalog configurations.

HyperVault Tables is documented in two places. This section covers building against it: the API reference, this quickstart, and connecting query engines. For running it — access control, table maintenance, Table Sharing, and disaster recovery — see the HyperVault Tables administration documentation.

Prerequisites

  • The HyperVault Client command-line tool configured with an alias for your cluster
  • Python 3.9 or later.
  • PyIceberg, PyArrow, and pandas.

You can install the required Python packages with the following command:

pip install pyiceberg pyarrow pandas

You must perform the following steps in the order specified.

Create the warehouse

A warehouse is the top-level container in HyperVault Tables that holds namespaces and tables. Creating a warehouse also creates a corresponding bucket to store Iceberg table data and metadata. You can inspect or manage the contents of this bucket only with the HyperVault Tables API or mc table commands. This protects the integrity of the underlying objects that contain your table data.

Create a warehouse named mywarehouse in the HyperVault cluster myhypervault:

mc table warehouse create myhypervault mywarehouse

Create the namespace

Namespaces organize tables within a warehouse. You can create as many namespaces as you need to manage multiple tables within a single warehouse.

Create a namespace named mynamespace inside the warehouse:

mc table namespace create myhypervault mywarehouse mynamespace

Create the table

Create a table with a schema defining the columns and their types, taking care to match not only the types of the expected fields but also whether or not a particular field must contain a value or can be empty. Schemas follow the Iceberg schema specification.

Create a table named mytable with five columns:

mc table create myhypervault mywarehouse mynamespace mytable                     \
  --schema '{"type":"struct","fields":[                                      \
            {"id":1,"name":"id","type":"long","required":true},              \
            {"id":2,"name":"name","type":"string","required":false},         \
            {"id":3,"name":"category","type":"string","required":false},     \
            {"id":4,"name":"price","type":"double","required":false},        \
            {"id":5,"name":"in_stock","type":"boolean","required":false}]}'

mc table create myhypervault mywarehouse mynamespace mytable \
  --schema '{"type":"struct","fields":[{"id":1,"name":"id","type":"long","required":true},{"id":2,"name":"name","type":"string","required":false},{"id":3,"name":"category","type":"string","required":false},{"id":4,"name":"price","type":"double","required":false},{"id":5,"name":"in_stock","type":"boolean","required":false}]}'

The schema defines these columns:

Column Type Required Description
id long Yes Unique identifier
name string No Product name
category string No Product category
price double No Product price
in_stock boolean No Whether item is in stock

You can verify the table was created with mc table list:

mc table list myhypervault mywarehouse mynamespace

View table metadata with mc table show:

mc table show myhypervault mywarehouse mynamespace mytable

The output resembles the following:

Table: mytable
Namespace: mynamespace
Warehouse: mywarehouse
Location: s3://mywarehouse/5e00905e-be0f-4799-8501-9dda7d48b695
Format Version: 2
Table UUID: 5e00905e-be0f-4799-8501-9dda7d48b695
Schema:
  - id: long (required)
  - name: string
  - category: string
  - price: double
  - in_stock: boolean

Run the sample application

Now that the table exists, you can work with it using the HyperVault Tables API.

Download the hello-hypervault-tables.py Python example and save it on your local system.

Run the example with the following command:

python hello-hypervault-tables.py

The script performs these operations:

  1. Connects to the HyperVault Tables catalog using SigV4 authentication.
  2. Loads the existing table created with mc table create.
  3. Displays the table schema and metadata.
  4. Appends three sample product records to the table.
  5. Queries the data using different filter expressions.

Expected output

The script produces output similar to:

============================================================
HyperVault Tables Basic Example
============================================================
Connected to catalog at http://localhost:9000/_iceberg
Loaded table: mynamespace.mytable

--- Table Information ---
Name: ('mynamespace', 'mytable')
Location: s3://mywarehouse/f07c5466-6929-46cd-b0f5-57335bd2fa09

Schema:
  id: long (required)
  name: string (nullable)
  category: string (nullable)
  price: double (nullable)
  in_stock: boolean (nullable)

============================================================
Appending Data
============================================================
Appended 3 rows to table
Loaded table: mynamespace.mytable

============================================================
Query Examples
============================================================

--- Query: All Rows ---
Found 3 total rows
    id      name     category  price  in_stock
0  101  Widget A  Electronics  29.99      True
1  102  Widget B  Electronics  49.99      True
2  103  Widget C     Hardware  19.99     False

--- Query: Filter 'price > 30' ---
Found 1 matching rows
    id      name     category  price  in_stock
0  102  Widget B  Electronics  49.99      True

--- Query: Filter 'in_stock = true' ---
Found 2 matching rows
    id      name     category  price  in_stock
0  101  Widget A  Electronics  29.99      True
1  102  Widget B  Electronics  49.99      True

--- Query: Filter 'category = 'Electronics'' ---
Found 2 matching rows
    id      name     category  price  in_stock
0  101  Widget A  Electronics  29.99      True
1  102  Widget B  Electronics  49.99      True

--- Query: Columns ('name', 'price') ---
Found 3 rows
       name  price
0  Widget A  29.99
1  Widget B  49.99
2  Widget C  19.99

--- Query: Columns ('name', 'price', 'in_stock') ---
    Filter: category = 'Electronics'
Found 2 rows
       name  price  in_stock
0  Widget A  29.99      True
1  Widget B  49.99      True

--- Query: Limit 5 rows ---
Retrieved 3 rows
    id      name     category  price  in_stock
0  101  Widget A  Electronics  29.99      True
1  102  Widget B  Electronics  49.99      True
2  103  Widget C     Hardware  19.99     False

============================================================
Snapshot After Append
============================================================

--- Snapshot Information ---
Snapshot ID: 3254159768753409734
Timestamp: 1769554450753
Operation: Operation.APPEND

============================================================
Example Complete
============================================================

Clean up

To delete the resources created in this tutorial, remove them in the reverse order they were created. Once you have removed all the HyperVault Tables resources for a warehouse, HyperVault converts the underlying bucket to a standard HyperVault bucket. You can then inspect or manage any remaining objects in the bucket with standard HyperVault Client commands such as mc ls.

# Remove the table
mc table remove myhypervault mywarehouse mynamespace mytable

# Optional: also permanently delete table files when removing the table
mc table remove myhypervault mywarehouse mynamespace mytable --purge

# Remove the namespace (must not contain tables)
mc table namespace remove myhypervault mywarehouse mynamespace

# Remove the warehouse (must not contain namespaces)
mc table warehouse remove myhypervault mywarehouse

# Optional: remove the warehouse bucket (must be empty and not linked to a table)
mc rb myhypervault/mywarehouse

title: HyperVault Tables API Reference | HyperVault Documentation
html:
HyperVault Tables API Reference

HyperVault Tables implements native Apache Iceberg tables support directly within HyperVault object storage, eliminating dependencies on external catalog services or metadata databases. The HyperVault Tables API is a REST interface that implements a subset of the Iceberg REST Catalog specification and adds endpoints of its own. For the endpoint-by-endpoint breakdown, see Supported endpoints and extensions.

Iceberg clients typically require a base path consisting of the HyperVault endpoint and catalog API path (https://hypervault.example.net:9000/_iceberg). Refer to the documentation for your preferred client, library, or application for specific behaviors around endpoint construction.

All API requests use the following base path:

http://example.net:9000/_iceberg/v1

Replace example.net with your HyperVault server hostname or IP address.

Supported endpoints and extensions

HyperVault Tables implements a subset of the Apache Iceberg REST Catalog specification and adds HyperVault extension endpoints of its own. The catalog classifies every route it registers as one or the other, and it advertises only the specification endpoints in the endpoints field of the catalog configuration response. The catalog serves both kinds of endpoint the same way, and both require the same authentication.

The following tables record which endpoints the catalog registers and how it classifies each one. They do not state how completely each operation is implemented.

Paths in these tables are relative to the base path /_iceberg/v1. The catalog is not the only table-related API HyperVault serves: sharing tables with an external consumer uses the Delta Sharing API, which has its own base path and its own documentation. See Delta Sharing.

Iceberg REST catalog endpoints

The catalog registers these endpoints as part of the Iceberg REST Catalog specification. Get catalog configuration lists them in its endpoints field, with {prefix} in place of {warehouse}.

Method Path Operation Description
POST /{warehouse}/namespaces CreateNamespace Create a namespace in a warehouse.
GET /{warehouse}/namespaces ListNamespaces List the namespaces in a warehouse.
GET /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace} GetNamespace Return namespace metadata and properties.
HEAD /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace} NamespaceExists Check whether a namespace exists.
DELETE /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace} DeleteNamespace Delete an empty namespace.
POST /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace}/properties UpdateNamespaceProperties Add, change, or remove namespace properties.
POST /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables CreateTable Create a table with a schema, partitioning, and properties.
GET /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables ListTables List the tables in a namespace.
POST /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace}/register RegisterTable Register an existing Iceberg table from its metadata file.
GET /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table} LoadTable Return table metadata, including schema and partition information.
HEAD /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table} TableExists Check whether a table exists.
POST /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table} CommitTable Apply table metadata updates atomically.
DELETE /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table} DeleteTable Delete a table, with optional purging of its data.
POST /{warehouse}/tables/rename RenameTable Rename a table, and optionally move it to another namespace.
POST /{warehouse}/transactions/commit CommitMultiTableTransaction Commit changes across several tables atomically.
POST /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}/metrics TableMetrics Accept a table scan metrics report from a client.
POST /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace}/views CreateView Create a view with a schema and a SQL definition.
GET /{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace}/views ListViews List the views in a namespace.

Specification endpoints the catalog does not serve

Released versions of the catalog register no route for the following specification endpoints:

Endpoint group Paths Effect on a client
Scan planning /plan, /plan/{plan-id}, /tasks The client plans scans itself.
Table credentials /credentials The client obtains storage credentials another way, such as an access key or a Security Token Service (STS) token.

Neither group appears in the endpoints field of Get catalog configuration. Read that field to determine what the catalog you are talking to actually serves, rather than assuming this table matches your version.

Intentional differences from the specification

HyperVault runs the Apache Iceberg REST Compatibility Kit against every release. The following behaviors differ from the specification on purpose, so the matching compatibility tests are excluded:

Behavior Difference
Slashes in names A table or namespace name cannot contain a slash.
Default column values Creating a table with a default column value is not supported.
Delete table purge default purgeRequested is a query parameter on the delete request. A delete that sets it to true, or omits it, removes the table metadata and its data files; a delete that sets it to false removes only the registry entry and the pointer, leaving the data intact. HyperVault defaults the parameter to true to work around a Spark client that omits it, and the Iceberg Java client also omits it when purge is false, so a request meant to preserve the data purges it. See apache/iceberg#11023.
Register table Re-registering a table whose data was purged fails, because the data files are gone.
Register view The compatibility suite’s view registration tests are excluded. Deleting a view takes no purge parameter and does not purge table data.
Custom view metadata location Creating a view with a custom metadata location is not supported.

AWS S3 Tables uses the term table bucket for the resource that HyperVault calls a warehouse. The catalog serves its warehouse encryption, warehouse tags, and warehouse maintenance endpoints under a second, /buckets path. The table-level endpoints have no /buckets path. The same handler serves both paths in each of the following pairs.

Authentication

All requests require AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) authentication with the service name s3tables. Requests must include standard AWS SigV4 headers:

  • Authorization - AWS SigV4 signature
  • X-Amz-Date - Request timestamp
  • X-Amz-Content-SHA256 - Payload hash

Example authentication flow

To authenticate a request:

  1. Create an HTTP request with method, URL, headers, and body.
  2. Calculate the payload hash (SHA256 of request body).
  3. Generate the SigV4 signature using your access key and secret key.
  4. Add the signature to the Authorization header.

Most AWS SDKs and libraries provide built-in SigV4 signing functionality. For example, the following Python code uses boto3and botocore:

from botocore.auth import SigV4Auth
from botocore.awsrequest import AWSRequest
import boto3

session = boto3.Session(
    aws_access_key_id='your-access-key',
    aws_secret_access_key='your-secret-key'
)

request = AWSRequest(
    method='POST',
    url='http://localhost:9000/_iceberg/v1/warehouses',
    data='{"name":"analytics"}',
    headers={'Content-Type': 'application/json'}
)

SigV4Auth(session.get_credentials(), 's3tables', 'region').add_auth(request)
HyperVault Tables uses standard HyperVault policy-based access control (PBAC) to define authorized actions on warehouses, namespaces, and tables. For more information about PBAC in HyperVault, see Access Control with Policy Management

Warehouse versioning

HyperVault creates the underlying warehouse bucket with versioning enabled and purge-on-delete configured. Iceberg relies on versioning to recover from failed transactions and to expire snapshots safely, so this configuration is applied automatically at warehouse creation. When you upgrade an existing bucket to a warehouse, the same versioning configuration is applied.

Because warehouse buckets require versioning, you cannot suspend versioning on a warehouse bucket. A PUT bucket-versioning request that attempts to set the Suspended state (or that supplies excluded prefixes) on a warehouse bucket is rejected with HTTP 400 Bad Request and the S3 error code InvalidBucketState (“This bucket is a Tables warehouse, versioning cannot be suspended.”).

Staged table creation

Setting stage-create to true creates the table as a draft. A staged table:

  • Is invisible to List tables and cannot be loaded with Get table metadata.
  • Returns a null metadata-location in the create response, which signals that the table is a draft without a final, queryable metadata location.

Finalize a staged table with a subsequent commit to the table endpoint (see Commit table changes). The commit marks the table as live, populates its metadata-location, and makes it visible to List tables. Staging lets you atomically create a table together with its first data commit.

Purge Behavior:

  • purgeRequested=false - Remove only catalog entry, preserving data files.
Default purge behavior differs from standard Iceberg

HyperVault Tables defaults purgeRequested to true, which differs from the standard Iceberg default of false. This is a deliberate choice for Spark compatibility.

The Iceberg Java client omits the purgeRequested parameter entirely when requesting a drop without purge (dropTable(identifier, false)). Because the parameter is omitted, the server applies its default of true, so dropping a table through Spark or the Java client deletes the data files even when the client intended to preserve them.

To drop a table without purging data files, explicitly pass purgeRequested=false in the query string:

DELETE /_iceberg/v1/{warehouse}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}?purgeRequested=false

The standard Iceberg Java client cannot send this parameter. Applications that require drop-without-purge should use PyIceberg or make a direct REST API call.

The catalog also advertises s3.delete-enabled=false through the Get catalog configuration endpoint to signal well-behaved clients not to attempt client-side file deletion.

Field Type Description

failureMessage string Error detail for a failed run. Omitted when the last run did not fail.

Listing with search and statistics

The List warehouses, List namespaces, and List tables operations support a case-insensitive substring search filter and an optional statistics mode intended for console and UI use.

Search filter

Add search to any list request to return only the entries whose name contains the given substring, matched case-insensitively. The filter works with both the default token-based pagination and the statistics mode described below.

GET /_iceberg/v1/analytics/namespaces/data_science/tables?search=order

Statistics mode

Add stats=true to a list request to include aggregate statistics for each returned entry and switch from token-based pagination to index-based pagination.

GET /_iceberg/v1/warehouses?stats=true&page=0&page_size=100&sort=size&sort_order=desc

Query parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description
stats boolean false Set to true to enable statistics mode. Required to use the page, page_size, sort, sort_order, and ui_token parameters; when set, the index-based page/page_size parameters replace the default token-based pageToken/pageSize. The search filter works in both modes.
page integer 0 Zero-based page index. The item offset is page * page_size.
page_size integer 100 Number of items per page. Values above 1000 are capped at 1000.
sort string name Statistic field to sort by. See the allowed values below. When omitted, entries are ordered by name.
sort_order string asc Sort direction - asc or desc.
search string - Case-insensitive substring filter applied to entry names.
ui_token string - Routing token returned by a previous response. Pass it back on subsequent page requests.

The allowed sort values depend on the entity being listed:

Operation Allowed sort values
List warehouses namespaces, tables, records, size
List namespaces tables, records, size
List tables records, size

When sort is omitted, entries are ordered by name.

Response headers:

Header Description
X-Minio-Ui-List-Token Routing token for the cached listing. Pass it back as ui_token on subsequent page requests so they reach the node that holds the cache.
X-Minio-Ui-Total-Count Total number of items matching the current search filter, for calculating the total page count.

In statistics mode, the response body adds a stats object keyed by entry name alongside the normal listing fields:

{
  "warehouses": ["analytics", "dev"],
  "stats": {
    "analytics": {
      "namespaces": 3,
      "tables": 12,
      "records": 4500000,
      "size": 892000000
    }
  }
}
