title: AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity | HyperVault Documentation
html:
AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity

The HyperVault Security Token Service (STS) AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity API endpoint generates temporary access credentials using Active Directory or LDAP user credentials. This page documents the HyperVault Server AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity endpoint. For instructions on implementing STS using an S3-compatible SDK, defer to the documentation for that SDK.

The HyperVault STS AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity API endpoint is modeled after the AWS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity endpoint and shares certain request/response elements. This page documents the HyperVault-specific syntax and links out to the AWS reference for all shared elements.

Request endpoint

The AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity endpoint has the following form:

POST https://hypervault.example.net?Action=AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity[&ARGS]

The following example uses all supported arguments. Replace the hypervault.example.net hostname with the appropriate URL for your HyperVault Server:

POST https://hypervault.example.net?Action=AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity
&LDAPUsername=USERNAME
&LDAPPassword=PASSWORD
&Version=2011-06-15
&Policy={}
&ConfigName=CONFIGNAME

Request query parameters

This endpoint supports the following query parameters:

Parameter Type Description
LDAPUsername string Required

Specify the username of the AD/LDAP user as whom you want to
authenticate.
LDAPPassword string Required

Specify the password for the LDAPUsername.
Version string Required

Specify 2011-06-15.
ConfigName string Optional

For deployments with multiple LDAP configurations, use this parameter to specify which LDAP provider to use for authentication.

If not specified, the endpoint uses the default configuration (registered internally as _).

Requires HyperVault Server version RELEASE.2025-12-20T04-58-37Z or later.
DurationSeconds integer Optional

Specify the number of seconds after which the temporary credentials
expire. Defaults to 3600.

- The minimum value is 900 or 15 minutes.
- The maximum value is 31536000 or 365 days.

If DurationSeconds is omitted, HyperVault checks the JWT token for an exp claim before using the default duration. See RFC 7519 4.1.4: Expiration Time Claim for more information on JSON web token expiration.
Policy string Optional

Specify the URL-encoded JSON-formatted policy to use as an inline session policy.

- The minimum string length is 1.
- The maximum string length is 2048.

The resulting permissions for the temporary credentials are the intersection between the policy matching the Distinguished Name (DN) of the LDAPUsername and the specified inline policy. Applications can only perform those operations for which they are explicitly authorized.

The inline policy can specify a subset of permissions allowed by the policy specified in the DN policy. Applications can never assume more privileges than those specified in the DN policy.

Omit to use only the DN policy.

See Access Management for more information on HyperVault authentication and authorization.
TokenRevokeType string Optional

A string to assign to the generated token that allows the token’s access to be revoked prior to expiration.

A user may have a maximum of 100 unique token revocation types at any time. A token revocation type can be assigned to multiple tokens.

Response elements

The XML response for this API endpoint is similar to the AWS AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity response. Specifically, HyperVault returns an AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentityResult object, where the AssumedRoleUser.Credentials object contains the temporary credentials generated by HyperVault:

  • AccessKeyId - The access key applications use for authentication.
  • SecretKeyId - The secret key applications use for authentication.
  • Expiration - The ISO-8601 date-time after which the credentials expire.
  • SessionToken - The session token applications use for authentication. Some SDKs may require this field when using temporary credentials.

The following example is similar to the response returned by the HyperVault Server STS AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity endpoint:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentityResponse xmlns="https://sts.amazonaws.com/doc/2011-06-15/">
<AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentityResult>
   <AssumedRoleUser>
      <Arn/>
      <AssumeRoleId/>
   </AssumedRoleUser>
   <Credentials>
      <AccessKeyId>Y4RJU1RNFGK48LGO9I2S</AccessKeyId>
      <SecretAccessKey>sYLRKS1Z7hSjluf6gEbb9066hnx315wHTiACPAjg</SecretAccessKey>
      <Expiration>2019-08-08T20:26:12Z</Expiration>
      <SessionToken>eyJhbGciOiJIUzUxMiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..ewHqKVFTaP-j_kgZrcOEKroNUjk10GEp8bqQjxBbYVovV0nHO985VnRESFbcT6XMDDKHZiWqN2vi_ETX_u3Q-w</SessionToken>
   </Credentials>
</AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentityResult>
<ResponseMetadata/>
</AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentityResponse>

Error elements

The XML error response for this API endpoint is similar to the AWS AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity response.

title: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity | HyperVault Documentation
html:
AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity

The HyperVault Security Token Service (STS) AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity API endpoint generates temporary access credentials using a JSON Web Token (JWT) returned from a configured OIDC Identity Provider (IDP). This page documents the HyperVault Server AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity endpoint. For instructions on implementing STS using an S3-compatible SDK, refer to the documentation for that SDK.

The HyperVault STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity API endpoint is modeled after the AWS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity endpoint and shares certain request/response elements. This page documents the HyperVault-specific syntax and links out to the AWS reference for all shared elements.

Request endpoint

The AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity endpoint has the following form:

POST https://hypervault.example.net?Action=AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity[&ARGS]

The following example uses all supported arguments. Replace the hypervault.example.net hostname with the appropriate URL for your HyperVault Server:

POST https://hypervault.example.net?Action=AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
&WebIdentityToken=TOKEN
&Version=2011-06-15
&DurationSeconds=86000
&Policy={}

Request query parameters

This endpoint supports the following query parameters:

Parameter Type Description
WebIdentityToken string Required

Specify the JSON Web Token (JWT) returned by the configured OpenID IDentity Provider.
Version string Required

Specify 2011-06-15.
DurationSeconds integer Optional

Specify the number of seconds after which the temporary credentials expire.

- The minimum value is 900 or 15 minutes.
- The maximum value is 31536000 or 365 days.

When the JWT has a usable exp claim and DurationSeconds is provided, DurationSeconds sets the credential lifetime and takes precedence over the exp claim.

When DurationSeconds is omitted, the credentials inherit their expiration from the JWT’s exp claim. When strict expiration is enabled (the default), the resulting lifetime must still fall within the minimum and maximum values above, or the request is rejected.

If the JWT has no usable exp claim, the request is rejected regardless of DurationSeconds, as described in the note below.

See RFC 7519 4.1.4: Expiration Time Claim for more information on JSON web token expiration.
Policy string Optional

Specify the URL-encoded JSON-formatted policy to use as an inline session policy.

- The minimum string length is 1.
- The maximum string length is 2048.

The resulting permissions for the temporary credentials are the intersection between the policy specified as part of the JWT claim and the specified inline policy. Applications can only perform those operations for which they are explicitly authorized.

The inline policy can specify a subset of permissions allowed by the policy specified in the JWT claim. Applications can never assume more privileges than those specified in the JWT claim policy.

Omit to use only the JWT claim policy.

See Access Management for more information on HyperVault authentication and authorization.

The role Amazon Resource Number (ARN) to use for all user authentication requests.
If used, there must be a matching OIDC RolePolicy defined for the RoleArn’s provider by the role_policy configuration parameter or the HYPERVAULT_IDENTITY_OPENID_ROLE_POLICY environment variable.

When used, all valid authorization requests assume the same set of permissions provided by the RolePolicy. You can use OpenID Policy Variables to create policies that programmatically manage what each individual user has access to.

If you do not supply a RoleArn, HyperVault attempts to authorize through a JWT-based claim.
TokenRevokeType string Optional

A string to assign to the generated token that allows the token’s access to be revoked prior to expiration.

A user may have a maximum of 100 unique token revocation types at any time. A token revocation type can be assigned to multiple tokens.
OIDC credentials must have a bounded expiration

HyperVault Server requires every credential issued from an OIDC login to derive a valid expiration from the identity token.

  • If the JWT includes a valid exp claim, the credential’s expiration is derived from it, unless you supply DurationSeconds, which takes precedence. When strict expiration (HYPERVAULT_STS_STRICT_EXPIRATION, enabled by default) is in effect, the resulting lifetime must fall within 900 and 31536000 seconds; when it is disabled, a lifetime derived from the JWT exp claim can fall outside those bounds.
  • If the JWT does not include a usable exp claim (missing, empty, or zero), the request is rejected with an ExpiredToken error. Supplying DurationSeconds does not change this.

This is a behavior change introduced in RELEASE.2026-07-24T16-43-31Z: in releases before it, a JWT without an exp claim was accepted and issued a non-expiring credential. If your identity provider issues tokens without an exp claim, configure it to include one.

Response elements

The XML response for this API endpoint is similar to the AWS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity response. Specifically, HyperVault returns an AssumeRoleWithWebIdentityResult object, where the AssumedRoleUser.Credentials object contains the temporary credentials generated by HyperVault:

  • AccessKeyId - The access key applications use for authentication.
  • SecretKeyId - The secret key applications use for authentication.
  • Expiration - The ISO-8601 date-time after which the credentials expire.
  • SessionToken - The session token applications use for authentication. Some SDKs may require this field when using temporary credentials.

   <AssumedRoleUser>
      <Arn/>
      <AssumeRoleId/>
   </AssumedRoleUser>
   <Credentials>
      <AccessKeyId>Y4RJU1RNFGK48LGO9I2S</AccessKeyId>
      <SecretAccessKey>sYLRKS1Z7hSjluf6gEbb9066hnx315wHTiACPAjg</SecretAccessKey>
      <Expiration>2019-08-08T20:26:12Z</Expiration>
      <SessionToken>eyJhbGciOiJIUzUxMiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..ewHqKVFTaP-j_kgZrcOEKroNUjk10GEp8bqQjxBbYVovV0nHO985VnRESFbcT6XMDDKHZiWqN2vi_ETX_u3Q-w</SessionToken>
   </Credentials>

The XML error response for this API endpoint is similar to the AWS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity response.

title: Transforms with Object Lambda | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Transforms with Object Lambda

HyperVault’s Object Lambda enables developers to programmatically transform objects on demand. You can transform objects as needed for your use case, such as redacting personally identifiable information (PII), enriching data with information from other sources, or converting between formats.

Overview

An Object Lambda handler is a small code module that transforms the contents of an object and returns the results. Like Amazon S3 Object Lambda functions, you trigger a HyperVault Object Lambda handler function with a GET request from an application. The handler retrieves the requested object from HyperVault, transforms it, and returns the modified data back to HyperVault to send to the original application. The original object remains unchanged.

Each handler is an independent process, and multiple handlers can transform the same data. This allows you to use the same object for different purposes without maintaining different versions of the original.

Object Lambda handlers

You can write a handler function in any language capable of sending and receiving HTTP requests. It must be able to:

  • Listen for an HTTP POST request.
  • Retrieve the original object using a URL.
  • Return the transformed contents and authorization tokens.

Create a function

A handler function should perform the following steps:

  1. Extract the object details from the incoming POST request.

    The getObjectContext property of the JSON request payload contains details about the original object. To construct the response, you need the following values:

    Value Description
    inputS3Url A presigned URL for the original object.
    The calling application generates the URL and sends it in the original request.
    This allows the handler to access the original object without the HyperVault credentials usually required.
    The URL is valid for one hour.
    outputRoute A token that allows HyperVault to validate the destination for the transformed object.
    Return this value with the response in an x-amz-request-route header.
    outputToken A token that allows HyperVault to validate the response.
    Return this value in the response in an x-amz-request-token header.

  2. Retrieve the original object from the HyperVault Server.

    Use the presigned URL to retrieve the object from the HyperVault Server. The contents of the object are in the body of the response.

  3. Transform the object as desired.

    Perform any operations needed to generate a transformed object. Since the calling application is waiting for a response, you may wish to avoid potentially long running operations.

  4. Construct a response containing the following information:

    • The transformed object contents.
    • An x-amz-request-route header with the outputRoute token.
    • An x-amz-request-token header with the outputToken token.

  5. Return the response back to Object Lambda.

    HyperVault validates the response and sends the transformed data back to the original calling application.

Manage the handler with settings

If you add or adjust these settings, restart HyperVault Server to apply the changes.

Register the handler

To enable HyperVault to call the handler, register the handler function as a webhook with the following hypervault server Object Lambda environment variables:

HYPERVAULT_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_ENABLE_functionname
Enable or disable Object Lambda for a handler function. For multiple handlers, set this environment variable for each function name.
HYPERVAULT_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_ENDPOINT_functionname
Register an endpoint for a handler function. For multiple handlers, set this environment variable for each function endpoint.

Authenticated endpoints

HyperVault supports the following environment variables for authenticated webhook endpoints:

HYPERVAULT_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_AUTH_TOKEN_functionname
Specify the opaque string or JWT authorization token for authenticating to the webhook.
HYPERVAULT_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_CLIENT_CERT_functionname
Specify the client certificate to use for mTLS authentication to the webhook.
HYPERVAULT_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_CLIENT_KEY_functionname
Specify the private key to use for mTLS authentication to the webhook.

Optional settings

HyperVault supports the following optional environment variable:

HYPERVAULT_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_RESPONSE_HEADER_TIMEOUT_functionname
Specify the timeout period for receiving response headers from the lambda webhook server. Specify a duration value such as 120s or 2m. Defaults to 0s (no timeout).
Version added
Requires HyperVault RELEASE.2025-08-29T21-27-49Z or later.

Trigger from an application

To request a transformed object from your application:

  1. Connect to the HyperVault Server.

  2. Set the Object Lambda target by adding a lambdaArn parameter with the ARN of the desired handler.

  3. Generate a presigned URL for the original object.

  4. Use the generated URL to retrieve the transformed object.

    HyperVault sends the request to the target Object Lambda handler. The handler returns the transformed contents back to HyperVault, which validates the response and sends it back to the application.

Example

Transform the contents of an object using Python, Go, and curl:

  • Create and register an Object Lambda handler.
  • Create a bucket and an object to transform.
  • Request and display the transformed object contents.

Prerequisites:

  • An existing HyperVault deployment
  • Working Python (3.8+) and Golang development environments
  • The HyperVault Go SDK

Create a handler

The sample handler, written in Python, retrieves the target object using a presigned URL generated by the caller. The handler then transforms the object’s contents and returns the new text. It uses the Flask web framework and Python 3.8+.

The following command installs Flask and other needed dependencies:

pip install flask requests

The handler calls swapcase() to change the case of each letter in the original text. It then sends the results back to HyperVault, which returns it to the caller.

from flask import Flask, request, abort, make_response
import requests

app = Flask(__name__)
@app.route('/', methods=['POST'])
def get_webhook():
   if request.method == 'POST':
      # Get the request event from the 'POST' call
      event = request.json

      # Get the object context
      object_context = event["getObjectContext"]

      # Get the presigned URL
      # Used to fetch the original object from HyperVault
      s3_url = object_context["inputS3Url"]

      # Extract the route and request tokens from the input context
      request_route = object_context["outputRoute"]
      request_token = object_context["outputToken"]

      # Get the original S3 object using the presigned URL
      r = requests.get(s3_url)
      original_object = r.content.decode('utf-8')

      # Transform the text in the object by swapping the case of each char
      transformed_object = original_object.swapcase()

      # Return the object back to Object Lambda, with required headers
      # This sends the transformed data to HyperVault
      # and then to the user
      resp = make_response(transformed_object, 200)
      resp.headers['x-amz-request-route'] = request_route
      resp.headers['x-amz-request-token'] = request_token
      return resp

   else:
      abort(400)

if __name__ == '__main__':
   app.run()

Start the handler

Use the following command to start the handler in your local development environment:

python lambda_handler.py

The output resembles the following:

 * Serving Flask app 'lambda_handler'
 * Debug mode: off
WARNING: This is a development server. Do not use it in a production deployment. Use a production WSGI server instead.
 * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000
Press CTRL+C to quit

Start HyperVault

Once the handler is running, start HyperVault with the HYPERVAULT_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_ENABLE and HYPERVAULT_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_ENDPOINT environment variables to register the function with HyperVault. To identify the specific Object Lambda handler, append the name of the function to the name of the environment variable.

The following command starts HyperVault in your local development environment:

HYPERVAULT_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_ENABLE_myfunction=on HYPERVAULT_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_ENDPOINT_myfunction=http://localhost:5000 hypervault server /data

Replace myfunction with the name of your handler function and /data with the location of the HyperVault directory for your local deployment. The output resembles the following:

HyperVault Object Storage Server
Copyright: 2015-2023 HyperVault, Inc.
License: GNU AGPLv3 <https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.html>
Version: RELEASE.2023-03-24T21-41-23Z (go1.19.7 linux/arm64)

Status:         1 Online, 0 Offline.
API: http://192.168.64.21:9000  http://127.0.0.1:9000
RootUser: hypervaultadmin
RootPass: hypervaultadmin
Object Lambda ARNs: arn:hypervault:s3-object-lambda::myfunction:webhook

Test the handler

To test the Lambda handler function, first create an object to transform. Then invoke the handler, in this case with curl, using the presigned URL from a Go function.

  1. Create a bucket and object for the handler to transform.

    mc alias set myhypervault/ http://localhost:9000 hypervaultadmin hypervaultadmin
mc mb myhypervault/myfunctionbucket
cat > testobject << EOF
Hello, World!
EOF
mc cp testobject myhypervault/myfunctionbucket/

  2. Invoke the Handler

    The following Go code uses the The HyperVault Go SDK to generate a presigned URL and print it to stdout.

    package main

import (
   "context"
   "log"
   "net/url"
   "time"
   "fmt"

   "github.com/hypervault/hypervault-go/v7"
   "github.com/hypervault/hypervault-go/v7/pkg/credentials"
)

func main() {

   // Connect to the HyperVault deployment
   s3Client, err := hypervault.New("localhost:9000", &hypervault.Options{
      Creds:  credentials.NewStaticV4("my_admin_user", "my_admin_password", ""),
      Secure: false,
   })
   if err != nil {
      log.Fatalln(err)
   }

   // Set the Lambda function target using its ARN
   reqParams := make(url.Values)
   reqParams.Set("lambdaArn", "arn:hypervault:s3-object-lambda::myfunction:webhook")

   // Generate a presigned url to access the original object
   presignedURL, err := s3Client.PresignedGetObject(context.Background(), "myfunctionbucket", "testobject", time.Duration(1000)*time.Second, reqParams)
   if err != nil {
      log.Fatalln(err)
   }

   // Print the URL to stdout
   fmt.Println(presignedURL)
}

    In the code above, replace the following values:

    • Replace my_admin_user and my_admin_password with user credentials for an HyperVault Server.
    • Replace myfunction with the same function name set in the HYPERVAULT_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_ENABLE and HYPERVAULT_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_ENDPOINT environment variables.

    To retrieve the transformed object, execute the Go code with curl to generate a GET request:

    curl -v $(go run presigned.go)

    curl runs the Go code and then retrieves the object with a GET request to the presigned URL. The output resembles the following:

License: GNU AGPLv3 <https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.html> Version: RELEASE.2023-03-24T21-41-23Z (go1.19.7 linux/arm64) Status: 1 Online, 0 Offline. API: http://192.168.64.21:9000 http://127.0.0.1:9000 RootUser: minioadmin RootPass: minioadmin Object Lambda ARNs: arn:minio:s3-object-lambda::myfunction:webhook Test the handler To test the Lambda handler function, first create an object to transform. Then invoke the handler, in this case with curl, using the presigned URL from a Go function. Create a bucket and object for the handler to transform. mc alias set myaistor/ http://localhost:9000 minioadmin minioadmin mc mb myaistor/myfunctionbucket cat > testobject << EOF Hello, World! EOF mc cp testobject myaistor/myfunctionbucket/ Invoke the Handler The following Go code uses the The MinIO Go SDK to generate a presigned URL and print it to stdout. package main import ( "context" "log" "net/url" "time" "fmt" "github.com/minio/minio-go/v7" "github.com/minio/minio-go/v7/pkg/credentials" ) func main() { // Connect to the MinIO deployment s3Client, err := minio.New("localhost:9000", &minio.Options{ Creds: credentials.NewStaticV4("my_admin_user", "my_admin_password", ""), Secure: false, }) if err != nil { log.Fatalln(err) } // Set the Lambda function target using its ARN reqParams := make(url.Values) reqParams.Set("lambdaArn", "arn:minio:s3-object-lambda::myfunction:webhook") // Generate a presigned url to access the original object presignedURL, err := s3Client.PresignedGetObject(context.Background(), "myfunctionbucket", "testobject", time.Duration(1000)*time.Second, reqParams) if err != nil { log.Fatalln(err) } // Print the URL to stdout fmt.Println(presignedURL) } In the code above, replace the following values: Replace my_admin_user and my_admin_password with user credentials for an AIStor Server. Replace myfunction with the same function name set in the MINIO_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_ENABLE and MINIO_LAMBDA_WEBHOOK_ENDPOINT environment variables. title: Installation | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Installation

Each subsection covers the installation and configuration methods for one supported platform.

To manage cryptographic keys for objects at rest, install a key management service. See the HyperVault KMS docs.

To manage container storage volumes in a Kubernetes environment, install DirectPV. See the HyperVault DirectPV docs.

Follow these three steps in order to create a new HyperVault cluster in any environment.

1) Deploy HyperVault

Create the baseline cluster, then confirm that your client producer and consumer processes can connect to it. This cluster is the foundation for the more advanced features you enable later.

Choose your platform:

  • Red Hat Enterprise Linux
  • Ubuntu Server Linux
  • Upstream “native” Kubernetes
  • Red Hat OpenShift Kubernetes
  • Apple macOS
  • Microsoft Windows
  • Container runtimes

Use HyperVault on macOS, Windows, or container hosts for local development and evaluation.

2) Enable network encryption

HyperVault supports Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2 or later for incoming and outgoing traffic. TLS requires at least one TLS certificate and its corresponding private key, covering the hostnames or IP addresses of the cluster.

Enable TLS on your platform:

  • Enable Network Encryption on Linux
  • Enable Network Encryption on Kubernetes

3) Configure server-side encryption

Connect HyperVault to a supported Key Management Service (KMS) such as HyperVault KMS to enable S3 Server-Side Encryption (SSE). HyperVault supports the SSE-KMS and SSE-S3 protocols with customer-managed keys stored on the KMS.

Enable SSE on your platform:

  • Enable Server-Side Encryption on Linux
  • Enable Server-Side Encryption on Kubernetes

Before you deploy

The checklists collect the hardware, software, and security settings to confirm before a production deployment, and align with the health checks SUBNET diagnostics run.

title: System tuning | HyperVault Documentation
html:
System tuning

Use the following checklist when tuning the hardware and operating system configuration for a production, distributed HyperVault deployment.

These settings align with the health checks performed by SUBNET diagnostics. Upload a diagnostic report with mc support diag ALIAS and review the results in SUBNET to validate your deployment against these recommendations.

CPU

Check Recommendation
CPU governor Set to performance on all nodes. Other governors (such as powersave or ondemand) reduce throughput under load. See CPU tuning.
Vector extensions Verify that SSE 4.2 and AVX2 extensions are available on all CPUs. HyperVault uses these for erasure coding and hashing. Check with lscpu | grep -i -E 'sse4_2|avx2'.
Minimum cores A minimum of 8 physical cores per node is recommended. Nodes with fewer cores may bottleneck under concurrent S3 workloads.
CPU consistency All nodes in the cluster should have the same CPU make, model, and core count. Asymmetric CPU configurations can cause uneven performance.

Memory

Check Recommendation
Swap Disable swap or set vm.swappiness=0. Swap causes unpredictable latency spikes. See Memory tuning.
Transparent huge pages Set to madvise, not always. The always setting can cause latency spikes and memory fragmentation. See Memory tuning.
IOMMU Disable IOMMU if not required for device passthrough. IOMMU adds overhead to DMA operations. Do not disable it on a host that serves S3 over RDMA into GPU memory, which needs PCIe peer-to-peer DMA. See Bootloader settings and Clear PCIe ACS redirect.
Memory consistency All nodes in the cluster should have the same amount of RAM. Asymmetric memory configurations can cause uneven performance.

Drives

Check Recommendation
XFS error retries Set max_retries to a finite value instead of the default -1 (infinite). Infinite retries can cause processes to hang on failing drives. See Disable XFS retry on error.
Mount options Mount XFS drives with noatime,nodiratime. This eliminates unnecessary access time updates on every read operation. See Storage requirements.
Drive usage Keep drive usage below 80%. Performance degrades as drives fill due to XFS fragmentation and reduced free extent availability. Monitor with mc support diag ALIAS.
Drive consistency All nodes should have the same number, type, and size of drives. Asymmetric drive configurations can cause uneven performance.

Network

Check Recommendation
Ethernet ring buffer Maximize RX and TX ring buffer sizes on all network interfaces used by HyperVault. Small ring buffers cause packet drops under load. See Ring buffers.
Internode latency Internode network round-trip time should remain below 10 ms. High latency impacts distributed lock performance and erasure coding operations. See Network tuning.
Network validation Validate network performance across all nodes before production deployment. See Network and storage performance testing.
RDMA fabric On a deployment using inter-node RDMA over a RoCE fabric, enable PFC end to end, DCQCN on every host NIC, and ECN with RED on every switch in the path. A lossy fabric collapses under the all-to-all erasure-write pattern. See Configure the RDMA fabric.

Operating system

Check Recommendation
Resource limits Set the open file descriptor limit to at least 65536 for the HyperVault process. Set LimitNOFILE=65536 in the systemd unit file or configure with ulimit -n 65536.
Process user Run HyperVault as a dedicated non-root user. Running as root is a security risk and is flagged by SUBNET diagnostics. See the installation guides for user creation steps.
Kernel stability Avoid kernel versions with known stability issues. See Linux Kernel Requirements.
OS consistency All nodes in the cluster should run the same operating system distribution and version. Mixed OS environments can introduce inconsistent behavior.

Validate with SUBNET diagnostics

After applying the above settings, upload a fresh diagnostic report:

mc support diag ALIAS

Review the results in SUBNET to confirm all checks pass. Address any remaining warnings before moving the deployment to production.

title: Security checklist | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Security checklist

Use the following checklist when planning the security configuration for a production, distributed HyperVault Server.

Required steps

Identity and access management

Step Details
Group policies Define group policies either on HyperVault or the selected 3rd party Identity Provider (LDAP/Active Directory or OpenID Connect)
Individual access policies Define individual access policies on HyperVault or the selected 3rd party Identity Provider
Identity provider configuration Configure HyperVault to use the selected 3rd party Identity Provider

Firewall access

Port Details
S3 API listen port Grant firewall access for TCP traffic to the Object Store S3 API Listen Port (Default: 9000)
Console port Grant firewall access for TCP traffic to the HyperVault Server console port (Recommended Default: 9443)

Encryption-at-rest

HyperVault supports Server-Side Encryption using HyperVault KMS:

Step Details
Install HyperVault KMS Download and install HyperVault KMS
Connect to HyperVault KMS Connect the Object Store to HyperVault KMS
Enable encryption Enable server side encryption on a bucket using mc encrypt set

HyperVault Server supports the following external KMS providers through the HyperVault Key Encryption Service (KES).

  • AWS Secrets Manager
  • Azure KeyVault
  • Entrust KeyControl
  • Fortanix SDKMS
  • Google Cloud Secret Manager
  • HashiCorp Vault
  • Thales CipherTrust Manager (formerly Gemalto KeySecure)

Encryption-in-transit (“in flight”)

TLS configuration

Step Details
Enable TLS Enable TLS for all HyperVault traffic
Certificate placement Configure certificate placement on each node
Domain certificates Add separate certificates and keys for each internal and external domain that accesses HyperVault
Key generation Generate public and private TLS keys using a supported cipher for TLS 1.3 or TLS 1.2
Trusted CA stores Configure trusted Certificate Authority (CA) store(s)
Kubernetes service Expose your Kubernetes service, such as with NGINX
Validate certificates
After configuring TLS, validate your certificates using a tool such as SSL Certificate Decoder.

title: Software checklist | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Software checklist

Use the following checklist when planning the software configuration for a production, distributed HyperVault deployment.

HyperVault pre-requisites

Operating system

HyperVault recommends a Linux kernel version of 6.8 or later for all new deployments to access critical performance features. Older 4.x and 5.x kernels run HyperVault and remain supported, but modern workloads and high-performance NVMe drives demand newer kernels to operate at peak efficiency.

The following distributions ship with a recommended kernel version by default:

Distribution Default Kernel
Ubuntu 24.04 LTS 6.8
RHEL 10 6.12
Rocky Linux 10 6.12
AlmaLinux 10 6.12
Oracle Linux 10 6.12
SUSE Linux 15 SP7 6.4

See recommended distributions for additional details, or the operating system compatibility matrix for the full supported range, including older RHEL and Ubuntu releases.

A deployment using RDMA acceleration needs the RDMA subsystem enabled in the kernel and these runtime libraries, which the RDMA package pulls in as dependencies:

Format Packages
DEB libibverbs1, librdmacm1, libnuma1
RPM libibverbs, rdma-core, numactl-libs

Filesystem

Drives must be formatted with the XFS filesystem. HyperVault requires XFS for best performance and consistency guarantees.

Unsupported filesystems
  • Do not use ext4. ext4 does not honor POSIX O_DIRECT/Fdatasync semantics and trades performance for consistency.
  • Do not use NFS volumes for distributed deployments. NFS is not strictly consistent. If you must use NFS in a distributed setup, use NFSv4 instead of NFSv3 for relatively better outcomes.
  • NFS can be safely used with single drive mode deployments.

See storage requirements for drive formatting and mount guidance.

Time synchronization

All servers in a distributed deployment must have clocks synchronized to within 15 minutes of each other. Use ntp, timedatectl, or timesyncd to synchronize time across nodes.

Check your operating system’s documentation for how to configure time synchronization.

System services

Disable or uninstall system services that index, scan, or audit the filesystem, system-level calls, or kernel-level calls. These services reduce performance due to resource contention or interception of HyperVault operations.

HyperVault strongly recommends disabling the following services on hosts running HyperVault:

  • mlocate or plocate
  • updatedb
  • auditd
  • Antivirus software (clamav)

The above list represents the most common services known to cause performance or behavioral issues with high performance systems like HyperVault. Consider removing or disabling any other service or software that functions similarly.

Alternatively, configure these services to ignore or exclude the HyperVault process and all drives or drive paths accessed by HyperVault.

Infrastructure and access

Requirement Details
System administrator access Root or sudo access to all remote servers in the deployment
Management tool A distributed systems tool such as Ansible, Terraform, or Kubernetes. Kubernetes deployments should use the HyperVault Operator.
Load balancer A load balancer to handle routing of requests, such as NGINX
Monitoring Prometheus or a Prometheus-compatible setup for metrics collection
Dashboard Grafana or a similar Prometheus-compatible visual dashboard
CLI mc installed on the local host system for command line management and support diagnostics

Release notes and artifacts

Review the HyperVault Release Notes before installing or upgrading. The release notes document changes, bug fixes, security updates, and any backwards-incompatible changes between versions.

Each release also publishes Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) files in CycloneDX and SPDX formats, along with a complete Go modules dependency list. Organizations that require supply chain transparency or vulnerability scanning can use these artifacts as part of their pre-deployment review.

See Release Artifacts for download links, feed subscriptions, and API access.

HyperVault install

Install a matching version of HyperVault across all nodes in the deployment.

Post-install tasks

Task Details
Create CLI aliases Create an mc alias for each server with mc alias set for command line access from a local machine
Bucket replication Configure bucket replication to preserve a copy of bucket contents to another location
Site replication Configure site replication to synchronize contents across multiple dispersed data center locations
Lifecycle management Configure object retention rules to manage when objects expire
Tiering Configure object tiering to move objects to warm or cold storage locations for cost efficiency

3rd party identity provider tasks

Task Details
Security Token Service Authenticate to HyperVault with STS. Enabling STS requires HyperVault support through SUBNET.

title: Deploy HyperVault as a Container | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Deploy HyperVault as a Container

HyperVault is licensed under the HyperVault Software License. An active license is required for production deployments.

This section documents steps for running HyperVault as a container.

Procedure

  1. Pull the latest stable image of HyperVault Server 

    docker pull quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault

    podman pull quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault

  2. Create the directory structure

    Create directories for data and certificates. The following example uses $HOME/hypervault as the base path.

    mkdir -p $HOME/hypervault/data $HOME/hypervault/certs

    Later steps mount these directories to standard Linux paths in the container.

  3. Retrieve your license file

    HyperVault requires a license to run. You can use an existing license, such as one from SUBNET, or you can request a new HyperVault Free Tier license.

    To request a new HyperVault Free Tier license, go to the HyperVault pricing page and select Get Started under the Free tier to obtain a free license. The free tier license allows you to run HyperVault on a single compute resource with one or more drives.

    Download the license file to $HOME/hypervault/hypervault.license for use in later steps.

    Free tier licenses do not include support. For support options, see the HyperVault pricing page. For more information about licenses, see Licenses.

  4. (Optional) Set up TLS

    If you need TLS for your deployment, configure it before starting the server. See Set up network encryption for instructions.

  5. Run the HyperVault Server in a container

    The following examples mount the local directories to standard Linux paths in the container:

    • $HOME/hypervault/data to /mnt/data for object storage
    • $HOME/hypervault/hypervault.license to /hypervault.license for the license file
    • $HOME/hypervault/certs to /etc/hypervault/certs for TLS certificates (if configured)
    docker run -dt                                             \
  -p 9000:9000 -p 9001:9001                                \
  -v $HOME/hypervault/data:/mnt/data                            \
  -v $HOME/hypervault/hypervault.license:/hypervault.license              \
  -v $HOME/hypervault/certs:/etc/hypervault/certs                    \
  --name "hypervault-server"                                   \
  quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault:latest hypervault server /mnt/data \
  --license /hypervault.license

docker logs hypervault-server

    podman run -dt                                             \
  -p 9000:9000 -p 9001:9001                                \
  -v $HOME/hypervault/data:/mnt/data                            \
  -v $HOME/hypervault/hypervault.license:/hypervault.license              \
  -v $HOME/hypervault/certs:/etc/hypervault/certs                    \
  --name "hypervault-server"                                   \
  quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault:latest hypervault server /mnt/data \
  --license /hypervault.license

podman logs hypervault-server

    The output of the logs command includes the startup message from the HyperVault Server. To access the server, use the localhost or 127.0.0.1 address on your local host machine.

  6. Install the HyperVault Client (mc)

title: Enable Network Encryption | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Enable Network Encryption

HyperVault implements Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2+ encryption with support for Server Name Indication (SNI) for selecting relevant TLS certificates in response to client requests.

You must set up TLS before you can enable data encryption, also called server-side encryption.

HyperVault supports the following types of certificate signatures:

  • self-signed

  • internal or private certificate authorities (CAs)

  • third-party CAs

Multiple certificates are implemented with SNI to determine which certificate to return to a client based on the hostname in the request.

This procedure uses the HyperVault certgen tool to generate self-signed certificates for local testing and development purposes.

If the private.key mounted into the container is password protected, set the HYPERVAULT_CERT_PASSWD environment variable so HyperVault can decrypt it at startup, and ensure the encrypted key uses the PKCS-1 format. See Encrypted private keys for the key conversion procedure.

Prerequisites

  • The certgen tool for generating self-signed certificates.
  • Alternatively, TLS certificates from your organization’s certificate authority.

Procedure

This procedure assumes you have

  • previously completed the Install HyperVault procedure.
  • have the necessary directories with full write access.
  • have a valid HyperVault License, such as the HyperVault Free license.

1. Generate TLS certificates

Use certgen to generate self-signed TLS certificates for testing and development. For production environments, use certificates issued by a trusted certificate authority.

Install certgen

Download the certgen binary for your platform from the releases page.

curl -L https://github.com/hypervault/certgen/releases/latest/download/certgen-linux-amd64 -o certgen
chmod +x certgen
sudo mv certgen /usr/local/bin/

curl -L https://github.com/hypervault/certgen/releases/latest/download/certgen-linux-arm64 -o certgen
chmod +x certgen
sudo mv certgen /usr/local/bin/

Generate certificates

Generate a certificate that includes the hostnames and IP addresses clients use to connect to HyperVault.

mkdir -p $HOME/hypervault/certs
cd $HOME/hypervault/certs
certgen -host "127.0.0.1,localhost"

This creates public.crt and private.key files in the $HOME/hypervault/certs directory.

For additional hostnames or IP addresses, include them as a comma-separated list:

certgen -host "127.0.0.1,localhost,hypervault.example.com,192.168.1.100"

2. Run HyperVault with TLS

Mount the certificate directory to the container to enable TLS. The following examples use the same directory structure as the installation procedure.

docker run -dt                                             \
  -p 9000:9000 -p 9001:9001                                \
  -v $HOME/hypervault/data:/mnt/data                            \
  -v $HOME/hypervault/certs:/etc/hypervault/certs                    \
  -v $HOME/hypervault/hypervault.license:/hypervault.license              \
  --name "hypervault-server"                                   \
  quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault:latest hypervault server /mnt/data \
  --license /hypervault.license                                 \
  --certs-dir /etc/hypervault/certs

docker logs hypervault-server

podman run -dt                                             \
  -p 9000:9000 -p 9001:9001                                \
  -v $HOME/hypervault/data:/mnt/data                            \
  -v $HOME/hypervault/certs:/etc/hypervault/certs                    \
  -v $HOME/hypervault/hypervault.license:/hypervault.license              \
  --name "hypervault-server"                                   \
  quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault:latest hypervault server /mnt/data \
  --license /hypervault.license                                 \
  --certs-dir /etc/hypervault/certs

podman logs hypervault-server

The --certs-dir flag tells HyperVault where to find the TLS certificates. HyperVault automatically enables TLS when it detects public.crt and private.key files in the specified directory.

3. Trust additional certificate authorities

If you need HyperVault to trust certificates from additional certificate authorities, such as when connecting to HyperVault KMS with self-signed certificates, place the CA certificates in the $HOME/hypervault/certs/CAs directory.

mkdir -p $HOME/hypervault/certs/CAs
cp /path/to/ca-certificate.crt $HOME/hypervault/certs/CAs/

When you start the container, the CA certificates are mounted to /etc/hypervault/certs/CAs and automatically trusted by HyperVault.

4. Connect using HTTPS

When TLS is enabled, use https:// instead of http:// when connecting to HyperVault.

Configure mc to trust the certificate

The mc client must trust the HyperVault server’s certificate. The self-signed certificate generated by certgen acts as both the certificate and Certificate Authority (CA). Copy the certificate to the mc configuration directory:

mkdir -p ~/.mc/certs/CAs
cp $HOME/hypervault/certs/public.crt ~/.mc/certs/CAs/

Then create an alias using HTTPS:

mc alias set myhypervault https://localhost:9000 hypervaultadmin hypervaultadmin

Alternatively, use the --insecure flag to skip certificate verification (not recommended for production):

mc alias set myhypervault https://localhost:9000 hypervaultadmin hypervaultadmin --insecure

Access the Console

Open your browser to https://localhost:9001 to access the Console.

When using self-signed certificates, your browser displays a security warning. You can proceed by accepting the certificate or add it to your system’s trusted certificates.

Recommendations for generating certificates

Supported TLS cipher suites

title: Enable FIPS Mode | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Enable FIPS Mode

Enable FIPS 140-3 ready cryptography for HyperVault deployments on Kubernetes.

When enabled, FIPS mode restricts cryptographic operations to algorithms that align with the Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) 140-3 program. Organizations subject to U.S. federal government compliance requirements, or those with similar regulatory needs, may require FIPS-aligned cryptography.

HyperVault FIPS mode uses Go’s native cryptographic module, which restricts operations to FIPS 140-3 approved algorithms. HyperVault makes no statements or representations regarding FIPS 140-3 certification status. Evaluate whether this implementation meets your specific compliance requirements.

Overview

HyperVault uses Go 1.24’s native FIPS 140-3 cryptographic module. Enable FIPS mode at runtime with the GODEBUG environment variable. There is no separate binary required.

With FIPS mode enabled, the following apply:

  • TLS connections use only AES-GCM cipher suites (CHACHA20-POLY1305 is excluded).
  • Object encryption (DARE) uses only AES-256-GCM.
  • SSH/SFTP connections exclude weak key exchange algorithms and non-compliant ciphers.
  • JWT operations use FIPS-validated SHA3 implementations.

Enable FIPS mode

FIPS mode requires setting the GODEBUG environment variable on both the HyperVault Operator and the Object Store pods.

HyperVault Operator

Version added
FIPS mode support in the HyperVault Operator requires Operator RELEASE.2025-12-16T20-51-03Z or later.

Modify the Operator Deployment to include the GODEBUG environment variable.

If you installed the Operator using Helm, create or update your values file:

env:
- name: GODEBUG
  value: "fips140=on"

Then upgrade the Operator Helm release:

helm upgrade hypervault hypervault/hypervault-operator \
  -n hypervault \
  -f hypervault-operator-values.yaml

Object Store

Add the GODEBUG environment variable to your Object Store deployment using the objectStore.env field in your Helm values:

objectStore:
  env:
  - name: GODEBUG
    value: "fips140=on"

Apply the configuration:

helm upgrade primary-object-store hypervault/hypervault-objectstore \
  -n primary-object-store \
  -f hypervault-objectstore-values.yaml

The Operator restarts the Object Store pods to apply the new environment variable.

Verify FIPS mode

Operator

Check the Operator version output for the FIPS indicator:

kubectl logs -n hypervault deployment/object-store-operator | grep -i version

When FIPS mode is active, the version string includes FIPS 140-3:

Version: RELEASE.2025-12-16T20-51-03Z FIPS 140-3

Object Store

Connect to the Object Store and check the server information:

mc admin info ALIAS

The output indicates FIPS mode status in the server details.

FIPS mode cipher restrictions

The following tables summarize which cryptographic algorithms are available in FIPS mode versus standard mode.

TLS cipher suites

Cipher Suite Standard Mode FIPS Mode
TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 (TLS 1.3) ✓ ✓
TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 (TLS 1.3) ✓ ✓
TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 (TLS 1.3) ✓ ✗
TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 ✓ ✓
TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 ✓ ✓
TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 ✓ ✓
TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 ✓ ✓
TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305 ✓ ✗
TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305 ✓ ✗

Object encryption (DARE)

Algorithm Standard Mode FIPS Mode
AES-256-GCM ✓ ✓
CHACHA20-POLY1305 ✓ ✗

Public key algorithms

Algorithm Standard Mode FIPS Mode
RSA (2048-4096 bit) ✓ ✓
ECDSA (P-256, P-384, P-521) ✓ ✓
EdDSA/Ed25519 ✓ ✗

Considerations

Certificate compatibility

Ensure your TLS certificates use FIPS-compatible algorithms. Certificates signed with EdDSA/Ed25519 are not compatible with FIPS mode. Use ECDSA with NIST P-256/P-384/P-521 curves or RSA keys instead.

Client compatibility

Clients connecting to a FIPS-enabled deployment must support the available cipher suites. Modern TLS clients generally support AES-GCM cipher suites, but verify compatibility with older clients if necessary.

Performance

AES-GCM cipher suites benefit from hardware acceleration on most modern CPUs (AES-NI instruction set). Performance impact from enabling FIPS mode is typically minimal on hardware with AES-NI support.

Related resources

  • Enable Network Encryption for TLS configuration
  • Operator Environment Variables for additional Operator configuration options

title: Install HyperVault | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Install HyperVault

HyperVault is licensed under the HyperVault Software License. An active license is required for production deployments.

Install on Kubernetes

Deploy HyperVault on Kubernetes

Install on OpenShift

Deploy HyperVault on OpenShift

Install using a private container registry

Deploy HyperVault using images stored in your own private container registry

Install in a fully airgapped environment

Deploy HyperVault to an airgapped environment

The guides in this section provide instructions for deploying HyperVault onto Kubernetes infrastructure. Installation should not be considered finished until you have completed the tutorials to enable network encryption and server-side-encryption.

Production hardware recommendations

When selecting hardware for your HyperVault Server implementation, take into account the following factors:

  • Expected amount of data to store at launch and growth in data storage for the next two years for total drive size
  • Expected growth in size of data for at least the next two years
  • Number of objects by average object size
  • Average retention time of data in years
  • Number of sites to be deployed
  • Number of expected buckets
  • Failure tolerance for drives and nodes

There is no exact formula useful for all situations. Consider your own needs for the above and create a architecture review discussion in SUBNET to discuss with HyperVault engineers and field architects.

Hardware consistency

HyperVault, like any distributed system, benefits from selecting identical configurations for all nodes in a given server pool. Ensure a consistent selection of hardware (CPU, memory, motherboard, storage adapters) and software (operating system, kernel settings, system services) across pool nodes.

Deployments may exhibit unpredictable performance if nodes have varying hardware or software configurations.

Checklist

The following checklist follows HyperVault’s Recommended Configuration for production deployments. The provided guidance is intended as a baseline and cannot replace SUBNET Performance Diagnostics, Architecture Reviews, and direct-to-engineering support.

Component Requirement Recommended
Storage Persistent volumes backed by adequate storage media 8+ Persistent Volumes
Network High speed network infrastructure 100GbE
CPU Server-grade CPUs with support for modern SIMD instructions (AVX-512), such as Intel® Xeon® Scalable or better 16+ vCPU per node
Memory Available memory to meet or exceed per-server usage by a reasonable buffer 128GB+ of available memory per node
Topology Node topology labels configured for spread zone distribution across failure domains Optional for production multi-rack or multi-AZ deployments

While HyperVault may run on less than the recommended hardware, any potential cost savings come at the risk of decreased reliability, performance, or overall functionality.

Required and optional images

HyperVault provides nine images for installing HyperVault with Helm.

Three of the images are required. The other six images provide optional services. Install any or all of the additional images as required.

Required images

HyperVault requires the following images:

Image Repository URL
operator quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/operator?tab=tags
hypervault quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault?tab=tags
hypervault-sidecar quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/hypervault-sidecar?tab=tags

Optional images

The following images are also available to enable specific features in HyperVault.

Image Usage Repository URL
kes Server-side encryption with KES quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/kes?tab=tags
kes-sidecar Server-side encryption with KES quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/kes-sidecar?tab=tags
mc Automating admin jobs quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/mc?tab=tags
aihub Storing AI models and datasets quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/aihub?tab=tags
prompt Using AI to query objects quay.io/hypervault/hypervault/prompt?tab=tags
warp Performing benchmark tests quay.io/hypervault/warp?tab=tags
If you plan to use optional features such as server-side encryption (KES), AI capabilities (AI Hub, Prompt), automation (mc), or benchmarking (warp), you must copy those optional images during the external preparation phase. Review the optional images table and copy all images for features you intend to use.

Optimizing performance

The following table shows areas that have the greatest impact on HyperVault performance, listed in order of importance.

Prioritize securing the necessary components for each of these areas before focusing on other hardware resources, such as compute-related constraints.

Infrastructure segment Description
Network Infrastructure Insufficient or limited throughput constrains performance
Storage Controller Old firmware, limited throughput, or failing hardware constrains performance and affects reliability
Storage (Drive) Old firmware, or slow/aging/failing hardware constrains performance and affects reliability

Additional recommendations

For other requirements, including for networking and memory, see recommended and system requirements.

For reviewing your existing hardware with tests, see recommended hardware tests.
